lessons.title: Chapter 1: What Is the Shell?
lessons.description: Understand what the shell is and how a terminal emulator gives access to it. Read the prompt, recall command history, and run the first simple commands like date, df, and free.
lessons.content:
# Chapter 1: What Is the Shell?

When we speak of the command line, we are really referring to the **shell**: a program that takes keyboard commands and passes them to the operating system to carry out. Almost all Linux distributions supply a shell program from the GNU Project called **bash**. The name is an acronym for *bourne-again shell*, a reference to the fact that bash is an enhanced replacement for **sh**, the original Unix shell program written by Steve Bourne.

## Terminal Emulators

When using a graphical user interface (GUI), we need another program called a **terminal emulator** to interact with the shell. KDE uses **konsole** and GNOME uses **gnome-terminal**, though it is likely called simply Terminal on your menu. They all basically do the same thing: give us access to the shell.

## Making Your First Keystrokes

Launch the terminal emulator and you should see something like this:

```bash
[me@linuxbox ~]$
```

This is called a **shell prompt**, and it appears whenever the shell is ready to accept input. It typically includes your username@machinename, followed by the current working directory and a dollar sign. If the last character of the prompt is a hash mark (#) rather than a dollar sign, the terminal session has **superuser privileges** — either you are logged in as the root user or your terminal emulator provides administrative privileges.

Try some typing. Enter some gibberish at the prompt:

```bash
[me@linuxbox ~]$ kaekfjaeifj
bash: kaekfjaeifj: command not found
[me@linuxbox ~]$
```

Because this command makes no sense, the shell tells us so and gives us another chance.

## Command History and Cursor Movement

Press the up arrow and the previous command reappears after the prompt. This is called **command history**. Most Linux distributions remember the last 1,000 commands by default. Press the down arrow and the previous command disappears. The left and right arrows position the cursor anywhere on the command line, which makes editing commands easy.

While the shell is all about the keyboard, the X Window System supports a quick copy-and-paste technique: highlight text with the mouse to copy it into an X buffer, then press the middle mouse button to paste it at the cursor. Don't be tempted to use ctrl-C and ctrl-V inside a terminal window — they don't work; those control codes have different meanings to the shell.

> The Console Behind the Curtain: Even with no terminal emulator running, several terminal sessions continue to run behind the graphical desktop. These **virtual consoles** are accessed by pressing ctrl-alt-F1 through ctrl-alt-F6, which presents a login prompt. Switch between them with alt-F1 through alt-F6, and on most systems return to the graphical desktop with alt-F7.

## Try Some Simple Commands

The `date` command displays the current time and date:

```bash
[me@linuxbox ~]$ date
Fri Feb 2 15:09:41 EST 2018
```

A related command is `cal`, which by default displays a calendar of the current month. To see the current amount of free space on our disk drives, enter `df`, and to display the amount of free memory, enter `free`:

```bash
[me@linuxbox ~]$ df
Filesystem              1K-blocks        Used Available Use% Mounted on
/dev/sda2                15115452     5012392   9949716 34% /
/dev/sda5                59631908    26545424  30008432 47% /home
[me@linuxbox ~]$ free
         total       used       free     shared    buffers     cached
Mem:    513712     503976       9736          0       5312     122916
Swap:  1052248     104712     947536
```

## Ending a Terminal Session

We can end a terminal session by closing the terminal emulator window, by entering the `exit` command at the shell prompt, or by pressing ctrl-D.

```bash
[me@linuxbox ~]$ exit
```

## Summary

- The shell is a program that takes keyboard commands and passes them to the operating system; bash is the GNU shell found on almost all Linux distributions.
- A terminal emulator gives us access to the shell from a graphical desktop.
- The shell prompt appears whenever the shell is ready for input; a trailing # instead of $ means superuser privileges.
- The up and down arrows recall command history, and the left and right arrows move the cursor for light command-line editing.
- Simple commands like date, cal, df, and free report the time, the calendar, free disk space, and free memory.
- A terminal session ends by closing the window, typing exit, or pressing ctrl-D.

lessons.title: Chapter 2: Navigation
lessons.description: Move around the Linux directory tree with pwd, cd, and ls. Distinguish absolute from relative pathnames and use the dot notations and the cd shortcuts.
lessons.content:
# Chapter 2: Navigation

This chapter introduces the three commands we use to move around the file system: `pwd` (print name of current working directory), `cd` (change directory), and `ls` (list directory contents).

## Understanding the File System Tree

Like Windows, a Unix-like operating system such as Linux organizes its files in a **hierarchical directory structure**: a tree-like pattern of directories which may contain files and other directories. The first directory in the file system is called the **root directory**, written as `/`. Unlike Windows, which has a separate file system tree for each storage device, Linux always has a **single** file system tree, no matter how many drives are attached; storage devices are mounted at various points on the tree.

## The Current Working Directory

The command line has no pictures, so imagine the file system is a maze shaped like an upside-down tree and we are able to stand in the middle of it. At any given time we are inside a single directory, called the **current working directory**. To display it, we use the `pwd` command:

```bash
[me@linuxbox ~]$ pwd
/home/me
```

When we first log in (or start a terminal session), our current working directory is set to our **home directory**. Each user account is given its own home directory, and it is the only place a regular user is allowed to write files.

## Listing the Contents of a Directory

To list the files and directories in the current working directory, we use `ls`:

```bash
[me@linuxbox ~]$ ls
Desktop Documents Music   Pictures   Public   Templates   Videos
```

## Changing the Current Working Directory

To change the working directory, type `cd` followed by the **pathname** — the route along the branches of the tree to the directory we want. Pathnames come in two flavors.

### Absolute Pathnames

An **absolute pathname** begins with the root directory and follows the tree branch by branch until the path is complete. The pathname `/usr/bin` means: from the root directory (the leading slash) there is a directory called `usr` that contains a directory called `bin`.

```bash
[me@linuxbox ~]$ cd /usr/bin
[me@linuxbox bin]$ pwd
/usr/bin
```

As a convenience, the prompt is usually set up to automatically display the name of the working directory.

### Relative Pathnames

A **relative pathname** starts from the working directory, using two special notations: `.` (dot) refers to the working directory itself and `..` (dot dot) refers to the working directory's **parent directory**.

```bash
[me@linuxbox bin]$ cd ..
[me@linuxbox usr]$ pwd
/usr
[me@linuxbox usr]$ cd ./bin
[me@linuxbox bin]$ pwd
/usr/bin
```

In almost all cases we can omit the `./` part because it is implied — `cd bin` does the same thing. Which form to use? The one that requires the least typing!

## Important Facts About Filenames

- Filenames that begin with a period are **hidden**; `ls` will not list them unless you say `ls -a`.
- Filenames and commands are **case sensitive**. The filenames File1 and file1 refer to different files.
- Limit punctuation in filenames you create to period, dash, and underscore. Do not embed spaces; use underscores to represent them.
- Linux has no concept of a "file extension". You may name files any way you like; contents are determined by other means.

## Some Helpful Shortcuts

| Shortcut | Result |
|---|---|
| `cd` | Changes the working directory to your home directory. |
| `cd -` | Changes the working directory to the previous working directory. |
| `cd ~user_name` | Changes the working directory to the home directory of user_name, e.g. `cd ~bob`. |

## Summary

- Linux organizes files in a single hierarchical directory tree rooted at `/`, regardless of how many storage devices are attached.
- The current working directory is where we "stand" in the tree; `pwd` displays it and login starts us in our home directory.
- `ls` lists the contents of the current working directory.
- `cd` changes the working directory using either absolute pathnames (from the root) or relative pathnames (from where we stand).
- The notations `.` and `..` refer to the working directory and its parent; `./` can almost always be omitted.
- Handy shortcuts: `cd` alone goes home, `cd -` goes back to the previous directory, and `cd ~user_name` goes to another user's home.


lessons.title: Chapter 3: Exploring the System
lessons.description: Use ls options and long format to inspect file attributes, determine file types with file, and read plain-text configuration files with a pager. Tour the standard directories of a Linux system.
lessons.content:
# Chapter 3: Exploring the System

This chapter adds three more commands — `ls` (list directory contents), `file` (determine file type), and `less` (view file contents) — and takes a guided tour of the Linux file system.

## More Fun with ls

Besides the current working directory, we can list any directory, and even multiple directories at once (`ls ~ /usr`). By adding `-l` we change the output to the **long format**, which reveals far more detail.

## Options and Arguments

A very important point about how most commands work:

```bash
command -options arguments
```

**Options** modify a command's behavior; **arguments** are the items the command acts on. Short options are a single character preceded by a dash (`-l`); many commands, including those from the GNU Project, also support **long options**, a word preceded by two dashes (`--reverse`). Multiple short options can be strung together, as in `ls -lt --reverse`. Command options, like filenames in Linux, are case sensitive. Common `ls` options:

| Option | Long option | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `-a` | `--all` | List all files, even hidden ones (names beginning with a period). |
| `-d` | `--directory` | List the directory itself rather than its contents. |
| `-F` | `--classify` | Append an indicator character (e.g. `/` for a directory). |
| `-h` | `--human-readable` | Display file sizes in human-readable format rather than in bytes. |
| `-l` |  | Display results in long format. |
| `-r` | `--reverse` | Display the results in reverse order. |
| `-S` |  | Sort results by file size. |
| `-t` |  | Sort by modification time. |

In long format the fields are: **access rights** (a leading `-` means a regular file, `d` a directory), the file's number of hard links, the owner's username, the owning group, the size in bytes, the date and time of last modification, and the name.

## Determining a File's Type with file

Filenames in Linux are not required to reflect a file's contents. The `file` command prints a brief description of what a file contains:

```bash
[me@linuxbox ~]$ file picture.jpg
picture.jpg: JPEG image data, JFIF standard 1.01
```

A common idea in Linux is that **"everything is a file"**.

## Viewing File Contents with less

Many files that contain system settings (**configuration files**) are stored as plain text, and `less` is a **pager** that displays them page by page, both forward and backward:

```bash
[me@linuxbox ~]$ less /etc/passwd
```

Press q to quit. On the course terminal the available pager is BusyBox `more`, which pages forward only.

> Less Is More: The `less` program was designed as an improved replacement of an earlier Unix program called `more`. The name is a play on the phrase "less is more". Whereas `more` could only page forward, `less` allows paging both directions.

## Taking a Guided Tour

The file system layout is specified in a published standard called the **Linux Filesystem Hierarchy Standard**. As we tour: `cd` into a directory, `ls -l` it, use `file` on interesting files, and view text files with a pager. Key directories:

| Directory | Comments |
|---|---|
| `/` | The root directory, where everything begins. |
| `/bin` | Programs that must be present for the system to boot and run. |
| `/dev` | Device nodes; "everything is a file" also applies to devices. |
| `/etc` | All the system-wide configuration files, e.g. `/etc/passwd`. |
| `/home` | Each user's home directory; ordinary users can write files only here. |
| `/proc` | A virtual file system maintained by the kernel; peepholes into it. |
| `/sbin` | "System" binaries reserved for the superuser. |
| `/tmp` | Storage of temporary, transient files. |
| `/usr` | The largest tree: programs and support files used by regular users. |
| `/var` | Data likely to change — databases, spool files, mail, and the `/var/log` log files. |

## Summary

- Most commands follow the pattern `command -options arguments`; short options can be strung together and long options start with `--`.
- `ls -l` reveals the long-format fields: access rights, hard link count, owner, group, size, modification date, and name.
- `file` determines a file's type, because filenames do not have to reflect contents — "everything is a file".
- Pagers like `less` let us read the plain-text configuration files that reveal how the system works.
- The tree follows the Filesystem Hierarchy Standard, from `/bin` and `/etc` to `/proc` and `/var/log`.
- The system is open for examination and study — in Linux there are no secrets.

lessons.title: Chapter 4: Manipulating Files and Directories
lessons.description: Create, copy, move, rename, and remove files and directories with mkdir, cp, mv, and rm, link them with ln, and select groups of files with wildcards.
lessons.content:
# Chapter 4: Manipulating Files and Directories

This chapter introduces five of the most frequently used Linux commands: `cp` (copy files and directories), `mv` (move/rename), `mkdir` (create directories), `rm` (remove), and `ln` (create hard and symbolic links). They beat a graphical file manager for power: `cp -u *.html destination` copies only HTML files missing or newer at the destination.

## Wildcards

The shell provides special characters called **wildcards** to specify groups of filenames rapidly. Using wildcards is also known as **globbing**.

| Wildcard | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `*` | Matches any characters |
| `?` | Matches any single character |
| `[characters]` | Matches any character that is a member of the set |
| `[!characters]` | Matches any character that is not a member of the set |
| `[[:class:]]` | Matches any character in the specified class |

Common character classes: `[:alnum:]`, `[:alpha:]`, `[:digit:]`, `[:lower:]`, `[:upper:]`. Patterns: `g*` matches any file beginning with g; `b*.txt` any file starting with b and ending in .txt.

## mkdir, cp, mv, rm

`mkdir dir1 dir2 dir3` creates one or more directories in a single command.

`cp item1 item2` copies one item to another; `cp item... directory` copies multiple items into a directory.

| Option | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `-a, --archive` | Copy files and all their attributes, including ownerships and permissions. |
| `-i, --interactive` | Prompt before overwriting; without it, cp silently overwrites. |
| `-r, --recursive` | Recursively copy directories and their contents. |
| `-u, --update` | Only copy files that don't exist or are newer in the destination. |
| `-v, --verbose` | Display informative messages as the copy is performed. |

`mv item1 item2` moves or renames item1 to item2; `mv item... directory` moves items into a directory. Either way the original filename no longer exists. mv shares `-i`, `-u`, and `-v` with cp. If dir2 does not exist, `mv dir1 dir2` renames dir1 to dir2; if it exists, dir1 moves inside.

`rm item...` removes (deletes) files and directories.

| Option | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `-i, --interactive` | Prompt before deleting; without it, rm silently deletes. |
| `-r, --recursive` | Recursively delete directories and their contents. |
| `-f, --force` | Ignore nonexistent files and do not prompt. |
| `-v, --verbose` | Display informative messages as the deletion is performed. |

> Be Careful with rm! Linux has no undelete command — once you delete something with rm, it's gone. A stray space in `rm * .html` deletes every file in the directory. When using wildcards with rm, test the wildcard first with `ls`.

## ln—Create Links

```bash
ln file link        # creates a hard link
ln -s item link     # creates a symbolic link
```

A **hard link** is an additional directory entry (name part) for the same inode (data part). It cannot reference a file outside its own file system or a directory. `ls -i` reveals the **inode number**, confirming that `fun` and `fun-hard` share one. A **symbolic link** is a special file containing a text pointer to the target — like a Windows shortcut, though it predates it. Delete the target and the link is **broken**; deleting a link removes only the link, not the target.

## Building a Playground

A safe place to practice:

```bash
[me@linuxbox playground]$ cp /etc/passwd .
[me@linuxbox playground]$ mv passwd fun
[me@linuxbox playground]$ mv fun dir1
[me@linuxbox playground]$ ln fun fun-hard
[me@linuxbox playground]$ ln -s fun fun-sym
[me@linuxbox playground]$ ln -s dir1 dir1-sym
[me@linuxbox playground]$ ls -l
total 16
drwxrwxr-x 2 me me 4096 dir1
lrwxrwxrwx 1 me me    4 dir1-sym -> dir1
-rw-r--r-- 4 me me 1650 fun
lrwxrwxrwx 1 me me    3 fun-sym -> fun
```

The leading `l` marks a symbolic link and `->` shows its target. Finally, `rm -r playground` removes the whole tree.

## Summary

- Wildcards (`*`, `?`, `[characters]`, `[!characters]`, `[[:class:]]`) select groups of filenames by pattern.
- `mkdir` creates directories and accepts multiple arguments in one command.
- `cp` copies; `-i` prompts, `-r` handles directories, `-u` copies only newer or missing files.
- `mv` both moves and renames; the original name ceases to exist afterward.
- `rm` deletes silently and permanently; use `-r` for directories and test wildcards with `ls` first.
- `ln` creates hard links (extra names sharing an inode) and, with `-s`, symbolic links (text pointers that break when the target goes).
- Perform the playground exercise over and over until it makes sense.

Inside the playground, create some files, use the `*.txt` wildcard with `cp`, create a symbolic link with `ln -s`, and remove the HTML file so you can confirm it is gone with `ls`.

lessons.title: Chapter 5: Working with Commands
lessons.description: Tell apart the four kinds of commands with type and which, find documentation with help and --help, and build your own commands with alias.
lessons.content:
# Chapter 5: Working with Commands

This chapter removes some of the mystery from commands and even creates our own, using `type`, `which`, `help`, `man`, `apropos`, `whatis`, and `alias`.

## What Exactly Are Commands?

A command can be one of four different things:

- An **executable program**, like the files in `/usr/bin` — compiled binaries such as those written in C, or scripts written in languages like the shell, Perl, Python, or Ruby.
- A command **built into the shell itself**; bash supports a number of commands internally called **shell builtins**. The `cd` command, for example, is a shell builtin.
- A **shell function** — a miniature shell script incorporated into the environment.
- An **alias** — a command we can define ourselves, built from other commands.

## Identifying Commands

The `type` builtin displays the kind of command the shell will execute:

```bash
[me@linuxbox ~]$ type type
type is a shell builtin
[me@linuxbox ~]$ type ls
ls is aliased to `ls --color=tty'
[me@linuxbox ~]$ type cp
cp is /bin/cp
```

The `which` command displays the exact location of an executable (`which ls` answers `/bin/ls`) but works **only** for executables. Given a builtin like `cd` it answers "no cd in (...)" — a fancy way of saying "command not found".

## Getting a Command's Documentation

- **help** — bash's built-in help for each shell builtin: `help cd`. In the syntax it prints, square brackets `[...]` indicate optional items and a vertical bar `|` indicates mutually exclusive items.
- **--help** — many executable programs display usage information, e.g. `mkdir --help`. Some don't support it, but try anyway; the error message often reveals the same information.
- **man** — most command line programs provide a formal piece of documentation called a **manual page**, viewed with the paging program `man`: `man ls`. Man pages hold a title, a synopsis, a description of the purpose, and a listing of options — a reference, not a tutorial.
- **apropos** — searches the list of man pages for a term: `apropos partition` lists every manual page mentioning partitions. `man -k` performs the same function.
- **whatis** — prints the name and a one-line description of a matching man page: `whatis ls` gives `ls (1) - list directory contents`.
- **info** — the GNU Project's alternative to man pages: hyperlinked like web pages, tree-structured into nodes of a single topic each. `info coreutils` opens the package menu.

The manual is broken into sections:

| Section | Contents |
|---|---|
| 1 | User commands |
| 2 | Programming interfaces for kernel system calls |
| 3 | Programming interfaces to the C library |
| 4 | Special files such as device nodes and drivers |
| 5 | File formats |
| 6 | Games and amusements |
| 7 | Miscellaneous |
| 8 | System administration commands |

To refer to a specific section, name it first: `man 5 passwd` describes the *format* of the `/etc/passwd` file, not the command. Many packages also install documentation into `/usr/share/doc`.

## Creating Our Own Commands with alias

First a small trick: more than one command can go on a line when separated by semicolons — `command1; command2; command3...`:

```bash
[me@linuxbox ~]$ cd /usr; ls; cd -
bin games include lib local sbin share src
/home/me
```

Check the name isn't taken with `type` (`test` is a shell builtin — oops; `foo` is free). Then define it:

```bash
[me@linuxbox ~]$ alias foo='cd /usr; ls; cd -'
[me@linuxbox ~]$ type foo
foo is aliased to `cd /usr; ls; cd -'
[me@linuxbox ~]$ unalias foo
```

The structure is `alias name='string'` — the name followed immediately (no whitespace allowed) by an equals sign and a quoted string. Aliasing an existing command to add a favorite option is common, as with `ls --color=tty`, and `alias` with no arguments lists them all. One tiny problem: command-line aliases vanish when the shell session ends.

## Summary

- A command is one of four things: an executable program, a shell builtin, a shell function, or an alias.
- `type` tells which kind the shell will execute; `which` shows an executable's location and nothing else.
- Documentation comes from `help` (builtins), `--help` (many programs), `man`/`apropos`/`whatis` (the sectioned manual), and `info` (GNU's hyperlinked manuals).
- `man 5 passwd` names a section explicitly: 1 for user commands, 5 for file formats, 8 for administration.
- Semicolons chain several commands on one line, and `alias name='string'` turns a chain into a new command.
- Command-line aliases disappear when the session ends.

exercises.title: Identify a command
exercises.instructions:
Find out what the shell will actually execute. Ask `type` about the builtin `cd` and about `ls`, and locate an executable with `which`.

```bash
type cd
type ls
which ls
```
exercises.hint: type reports builtins, aliases, and file paths; which only answers for executable programs.

verification_rules.feedback_on_failure: Run `type cd`; cd is a shell builtin, so the answer should contain the word builtin.
Run `which ls`; it should print the path of the ls executable, something ending in /ls.

exercises.title: Create an alias
exercises.instructions:
Chain commands with semicolons and give the sequence a name. First check the alias name is free with `type`, then define it and confirm it with `type` again.

```bash
type ll
alias ll='ls -l ~'
type ll
```
exercises.hint: Remember the structure `alias name='string'` with no whitespace around the equals sign.

verification_rules.feedback_on_failure: Run `alias ll='ls -l ~'` exactly as shown to define the alias.
Run `type ll`; while the alias is defined in this session, type reports it as an alias.

lessons.title: Chapter 6: Redirection
lessons.description: Redirect stdout, stderr, and stdin with >, >>, 2>, and <, discard output into /dev/null, and chain filters such as sort, grep, wc, head, tail, and tee into pipelines.
lessons.content:
# Chapter 6: Redirection

This lesson unleashes what may be the coolest feature of the command line: **I/O redirection** — redirecting commands' input and output to and from files, and chaining commands into **pipelines**. We introduce `cat`, `sort`, `uniq`, `grep`, `wc`, `head`, `tail`, and `tee`.

## Standard Input, Output, and Error

Programs such as `ls` send their results to a special file called **standard output** (**stdout**) and their status and error messages to **standard error** (**stderr**); by default both are linked to the screen. Many programs read from **standard input** (**stdin**), attached to the keyboard. The shell references these streams as **file descriptors 0, 1, and 2**.

## Redirecting Standard Output

To redirect standard output to a file instead of the screen we use the `>` operator:

```bash
[me@linuxbox ~]$ ls -l /usr/bin > ls-output.txt
```

Testing with a nonexistent directory shows a twist:

```bash
[me@linuxbox ~]$ ls -l /bin/usr > ls-output.txt
ls: cannot access /bin/usr: No such file or directory
```

The error still appears, because ls sends errors to standard error, not stdout — and the file now has zero length, because `>` always rewrites the destination from the beginning. A bare `> ls-output.txt` truncates a file or creates an empty one. To append instead, use `>>`: `ls -l /usr/bin >> ls-output.txt`.

## Redirecting Standard Error

Standard error needs its file descriptor number:

```bash
[me@linuxbox ~]$ ls -l /bin/usr 2> ls-error.txt
```

To capture everything in one file, the traditional form performs two redirections — stdout to the file, then descriptor 2 to descriptor 1:

```bash
[me@linuxbox ~]$ ls -l /bin/usr > ls-output.txt 2>&1
```

> Notice That the Order of the Redirections Is Significant: The redirection of standard error must occur after redirecting standard output or it doesn't work; written `2>&1 >ls-output.txt`, stderr goes to the screen.

Recent bash versions streamline this to `&>` (and `&>>` to append). Sometimes silence is golden: `/dev/null`, the **bit bucket**, accepts input and does nothing, so `ls -l /bin/usr 2> /dev/null` discards the error.

## Redirecting Standard Input

`cat` reads one or more files and copies them to standard output. Given no arguments it reads stdin, echoing each line until ctrl-D signals **end of file (EOF)**. It can join files (`cat movie.mpeg.0* > movie.mpeg`; wildcards expand sorted) and create text files:

```bash
[me@linuxbox ~]$ cat > lazy_dog.txt
The quick brown fox jumped over the lazy dog.
```

Type ctrl-D and we have implemented the world's dumbest word processor. The `<` operator changes the source of stdin from the keyboard to a file: `cat < lazy_dog.txt`.

## Pipelines and Filters

Using the **pipe operator** `|`, one command's stdout becomes another command's stdin: `command1 | command2`. Commands used this way are **filters** — they take input, change it, and output it.

```bash
[me@linuxbox ~]$ ls /bin /usr/bin | sort | uniq | less
```

`sort` merges the listings into one sorted list; `uniq` removes duplicates (`-d` shows only the duplicates). `wc` prints line, word, and byte counts; `wc -l` in a pipeline counts things. `grep pattern filename` prints matching lines; `-i` ignores case, `-v` inverts the match. `head` prints the first 10 lines and `tail` the last 10, adjustable with `-n`; `tail -f` follows a growing log file in real time until ctrl-C. `tee` creates a "tee" fitting on our pipe, copying stdin to both stdout and one or more files:

```bash
[me@linuxbox ~]$ ls /usr/bin | tee ls.txt | grep zip
bunzip2
bzip2
gunzip
```

> The Difference Between > and |: Redirection connects a command with a file; a pipeline connects one command's output to another command's input. A reader, as superuser in /usr/bin, typed `ls > less` — `>` silently overwrote the less *program* with the listing text. Treat it with a lot of respect.

## Summary

- Programs write results to stdout, errors to stderr, and read stdin: file descriptors 0, 1, and 2.
- `>` redirects stdout and always rewrites the destination from the beginning; `>>` appends; a bare `>` truncates a file.
- `2>` redirects stderr; `> file 2>&1` captures both, and the order matters; bash also offers `&>` and `&>>`.
- `/dev/null` is the bit bucket that discards any output sent to it.
- `<` redirects a file into stdin; `cat` with no arguments reads stdin — "the world's dumbest word processor".
- Pipelines chain filters — `sort`, `uniq`, `grep`, `wc`, `head`, `tail`, and `tee` — transforming data in transit.


lessons.title: Chapter 7: Seeing the World as the Shell Sees It
lessons.description: You can predict what the shell does to a command line before it runs—pathname, tilde, arithmetic, brace and parameter expansion, and command substitution—and use quoting to suppress the expansions you don't want.
lessons.content:
# Chapter 7: Seeing the World as the Shell Sees It

When we press the enter key, bash performs several substitutions on the text of a command before it carries it out. This process is called **expansion**: we enter something and it is expanded into something else before the shell acts on it. One new command demonstrates it all: `echo`, a shell builtin that prints its text arguments on standard output.

```bash
[me@linuxbox ~]$ echo this is a test
this is a test
[me@linuxbox ~]$ echo *
Desktop Documents ls-output.txt Music Pictures Public Templates Videos
```

The `echo` command never saw the `*`; the shell had already expanded it into the names of the files in the current working directory.

## Pathname Expansion

The mechanism by which wildcards work is called **pathname expansion**. In the home directory from the example:

```bash
[me@linuxbox ~]$ echo D*
Desktop Documents
[me@linuxbox ~]$ echo [[:upper:]]*
Desktop Documents Music Pictures Public Templates Videos
[me@linuxbox ~]$ echo /usr/*/share
/usr/kerberos/share /usr/local/share
```

> **Hidden files.** Period-prefixed names are hidden from expansion: `echo *` does not reveal them, and `echo .*` also produces `.` and `..` (the current and parent directories). Use `echo .[!.]*` or `ls -A` ("almost all") for a correct listing.

## Tilde and Arithmetic Expansion

At the beginning of a word, `~` expands into the home directory of the named user, or of the current user if none is named: `echo ~` gives `/home/me`, `echo ~foo` gives `/home/foo`.

**Arithmetic expansion** has the form `$((expression))` and turns the shell prompt into a calculator, integers only:

| Operator | Description |
|---|---|
| + | Addition |
| - | Subtraction |
| * | Multiplication |
| / | Division (integer results) |
| % | Modulo ("remainder") |
| ** | Exponentiation |

```bash
[me@linuxbox ~]$ echo $((2 + 2))
4
[me@linuxbox ~]$ echo Five divided by two equals $((5/2)) with $((5%2)) left over.
Five divided by two equals 2 with 1 left over.
```

Spaces are not significant; parentheses group subexpressions (`echo $(((5**2) * 3))` prints 75).

## Brace Expansion

**Brace expansion** creates multiple text strings from a pattern with a preamble, a braced comma-separated list or range of integers or characters, and a postscript; no unquoted whitespace:

```bash
[me@linuxbox ~]$ echo Front-{A,B,C}-Back
Front-A-Back Front-B-Back Front-C-Back
[me@linuxbox ~]$ echo Number_{1..5}
Number_1 Number_2 Number_3 Number_4 Number_5
```

Ranges can be zero-padded (`{01..15}`) and nested (`a{A{1,2},B{3,4}}b`). The classic use is generating directory lists that sort chronologically: `mkdir {2007..2009}-{01..12}`.

## Parameter Expansion and Command Substitution

**Parameter expansion** reveals **variables**, named chunks of data the system stores: `echo $USER` prints your username, and `printenv | less` lists them. A misspelled variable name expands to an empty string.

**Command substitution** uses command output as an expansion: `ls -l $(which cp)` lists cp's real file without knowing its pathname. Entire pipelines work too; the older alternate syntax encloses the command in backquotes.

## Quoting

**Quoting** selectively suppresses unwanted expansions. Inside **double quotes**, all special characters lose their meaning except `$`, backslash and backtick: word splitting, pathname, tilde and brace expansion are suppressed, while parameter, arithmetic and command substitution still happen. Files with embedded spaces need it: unquoted `ls -l two words.txt` fails twice; `ls -l "two words.txt"` works. Word splitting treats unquoted spaces, tabs and newlines as delimiters, so `echo $(cal)` collapses the calendar to one line (38 arguments) while `echo "$(cal)"` keeps one argument.

**Single quotes** suppress all expansions; each level of quoting suppresses more:

```bash
[me@linuxbox ~]$ echo text ~/*.txt {a,b} $(echo foo) $((2+2)) $USER
text /home/me/ls-output.txt a b foo 4 me
[me@linuxbox ~]$ echo "text ~/*.txt {a,b} $(echo foo) $((2+2)) $USER"
text ~/*.txt {a,b} foo 4 me
[me@linuxbox ~]$ echo 'text ~/*.txt {a,b} $(echo foo) $((2+2)) $USER'
text ~/*.txt {a,b} $(echo foo) $((2+2)) $USER
```

To quote one character, precede it with a backslash, the **escape character**: `echo "The balance for user $USER is: \$5.00"` or `mv bad\&filename good_filename`. Backslash also introduces **escape sequences** for control codes:

| Escape sequence | Meaning |
|---|---|
| \a | Bell (an alert that causes the computer to beep) |
| \b | Backspace |
| \n | Newline; a line feed on Unix-like systems |
| \r | Carriage return |
| \t | Tab |

`echo -e` (and `$' '`) interprets them: `sleep 10; echo -e "Time's up\a"` is a primitive countdown timer.

## Summary

- Pressing enter triggers expansion before the command runs: pathname, tilde, arithmetic, brace, parameter, command substitution.
- `echo` makes expansions visible—why `echo *` prints filenames, not a star.
- Double quotes suppress word splitting and most expansions but keep `$`, backslash and backtick active; single quotes suppress all; a backslash escapes one character.
- Expansion and quoting are arguably the shell's most important subjects; without them much of its potential power is wasted.

lessons.title: Chapter 8: Advanced Keyboard Tricks
lessons.description: You can edit long command lines without retyping them using Readline cursor and kill/yank keys, complete names with tab, and recall previous commands with ctrl-R and history expansion.
lessons.content:
# Chapter 8: Advanced Keyboard Tricks

The command line prizes laziness—doing the most work with the fewest keystrokes—and never lifting your fingers from the keyboard for the mouse. bash implements command line editing with a library called **Readline**; this chapter introduces `clear` (clear the terminal screen) and `history` (display or manipulate the history list).

> **Note.** Some key sequences, particularly alt combinations, may be intercepted by the GUI; all work properly on a virtual console.

## Cursor Movement

| Key | Action |
|---|---|
| ctrl-A / ctrl-E | Move cursor to the beginning / end of the line. |
| ctrl-F / ctrl-B | Forward / backward one character; same as the arrow keys. |
| alt-F / alt-B | Forward / backward one word. |
| ctrl-L | Clear the screen and move the cursor to the top-left corner; `clear` does the same. |

## Modifying Text

| Key | Action |
|---|---|
| ctrl-D | Delete the character at the cursor location. |
| ctrl-T / alt-T | Transpose (exchange) the character / word at the cursor with the one preceding it. |
| alt-L / alt-U | Lowercase / uppercase the characters from the cursor to the end of the word. |

## Cutting and Pasting (Killing and Yanking) Text

Readline calls cutting and pasting **killing** and **yanking**; killed text is stored in a buffer called the **kill-ring**.

| Key | Action |
|---|---|
| ctrl-K | Kill text from the cursor to the end of line. |
| ctrl-U | Kill text from the cursor to the beginning of the line. |
| alt-D | Kill text from the cursor to the end of the current word. |
| alt-backspace | Kill to the beginning of the current word; at a word's start, kill the previous word. |
| ctrl-Y | Yank text from the kill-ring at the cursor location. |

Readline names alt the **meta key**: its developers could not assume every terminal had an extra control key, so they invented one. Pressing and releasing esc equals holding alt.

## Completion

Pressing tab while typing a command triggers **completion**: `ls l` + tab becomes `ls ls-output.txt`, while `ls D` + tab completes nothing because D matches more than one entry—the clue must be unambiguous (`ls Do` completes to Documents). Completion works on pathnames, variables (leading `$`), usernames (`~`), commands (first word) and hostnames (`@`, from /etc/hosts).

| Key | Action |
|---|---|
| alt-? | Display a list of possible completions; pressing tab a second time usually does the same. |
| alt-* | Insert all possible completions, useful when you want more than one match. |

Bash also has **programmable completion**—application-specific rules implemented as shell functions; `set | less` shows them.

## Using History

bash stores entered commands in the file `bash_history` in your home directory—the last 500 by default, though most distributions keep 1,000:

```bash
[me@linuxbox ~]$ history | grep /usr/bin
   88   ls -l /usr/bin > ls-output.txt
[me@linuxbox ~]$ !88
```

The `!88` is **history expansion**: bash substitutes the 88th item of the history list. For incremental searching, press ctrl-R and start typing; the prompt becomes `(reverse-i-search)`'/usr/bin': ls -l /usr/bin > ls-output.txt`. It is "reverse" because we search from now into the past. Press enter to execute the match, ctrl-J to copy it to the command line, ctrl-R for the next occurrence, or ctrl-G/ctrl-C to quit.

| Key | Action |
|---|---|
| ctrl-P / ctrl-N | Move to the previous / next history entry; same as the up / down arrows. |
| alt-< / alt-> | Move to the top / bottom of the history list. |
| ctrl-R | Reverse incremental search. |
| alt-P / alt-N | Reverse / forward search, nonincremental: type the string, then enter. |
| ctrl-O | Execute the current history item and advance to the next—handy for re-running a sequence. |

## History Expansion

| Sequence | Action |
|---|---|
| !! | Repeat the last command (easier with the up arrow and enter). |
| !number | Repeat history list item number. |
| !string | Repeat last history list item starting with string. |
| !?string | Repeat last history list item containing string. |

Use the `!string` and `!?string` forms only when you are absolutely sure of the history's contents; the rest of the mechanism is arcane and documented in the "HISTORY EXPANSION" section of the bash man page.

## Recording a Session

Most distributions include `script`, which records an entire shell session into a file: `script file`, defaulting to a file named `typescript`.

## Summary

- Readline keys move the cursor by character and word, jump to line ends, and transpose or re-case text without retyping.
- Killing and yanking (ctrl-K, ctrl-U, ctrl-Y with the kill-ring) is the command line's cut and paste.
- Tab completion finishes unambiguous names; a second tab or alt-? shows the options.
- bash_history holds past commands; ctrl-R searches it incrementally, ctrl-P/N walk it, and history expansion (!! and !number) re-runs entries.
- These tricks are optional but potentially helpful—pick and choose as desired.


Then reuse that line from history rather than retyping it: press ctrl-R, start typing `echo tab`, and when the found line appears press ctrl-J to copy it onto the command line; edit it to read `echo ctrl-R searched the history` and append it to the same file with `>>`. Finally run `history` to see the numbered list of commands you have entered.

lessons.title: Chapter 9: Permissions
lessons.description: You can read and change file modes in octal and symbolic notation, control default permissions with umask, recognize the special file bits, and apply the book's shared-directory permission workflow as the superuser.
lessons.content:
# Chapter 9: Permissions

Linux is a **multiuser** system: one user may not crash the machine or interfere with another's files, so users must be protected from each other. This chapter introduces that essential part of system security with the commands `id`, `chmod`, `umask`, `su`, `sudo`, `chown`, `chgrp` and `passwd`.

## Owners, Group Members, and Everybody Else

A regular user cannot read `/etc/shadow`: "Permission denied." In the Unix security model a **user** owns files and controls access, users belong to a **group** granted access by owners, and owners may grant rights to everybody—the **world**. `id` reports your identity:

```bash
[me@linuxbox ~]$ id
uid=500(me) gid=500(me) groups=500(me)
```

Accounts get a **user ID (uid)** and **group ID (gid)**: `/etc/passwd` defines users (name, uid, gid, real name, home, shell), `/etc/group` defines groups, `/etc/shadow` holds passwords; all list the superuser (uid 0) and system users.

## Reading, Writing, and Executing

In `ls -l` output the first attribute character is the file type: `-` regular file, `d` directory, `l` symbolic link (its attributes are dummies; the real ones belong to the target), `c` character special file (byte streams like /dev/null), `b` block special file (hard drives). The next nine characters are the **file mode**: read, write and execute for owner, group and world.

| Attribute | Files | Directories |
|---|---|---|
| r | Open and read the file. | List the contents if execute is also set. |
| w | Write or truncate; deleting and renaming is governed by directory attributes. | Create, delete and rename files inside if execute is also set. |
| x | Run as a program; scripts must also be readable. | Enter the directory, e.g. `cd directory`. |

## chmod: Change File Mode

Only a file's owner or the superuser may change its mode. In **octal notation** each digit represents three binary digits:

| Octal | Binary | File mode |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | 000 | --- |
| 1 | 001 | --x |
| 2 | 010 | -w- |
| 3 | 011 | -wx |
| 4 | 100 | r-- |
| 5 | 101 | r-x |
| 6 | 110 | rw- |
| 7 | 111 | rwx |

```bash
[me@linuxbox ~]$ chmod 600 foo.txt
[me@linuxbox ~]$ ls -l foo.txt
-rw------- 1 me    me   0 2018-03-06 14:52 foo.txt
```

Three digits set owner, group and world; you mostly need 7 (rwx), 6 (rw-), 5 (r-x), 4 (r--) and 0 (---). **Symbolic notation** combines who—`u` owner, `g` group, `o` others, `a` all (default)—an operation—`+`, `-`, `=`—and r, w, x: `u+x` adds owner execute, `+x` equals `a+x`, `go=rw` sets group and others to read/write, and `u+x,go=rx` chains with commas. Symbolic notation changes one attribute at a time; `--recursive` hits files and directories alike, rarely wanted.

## umask: Set Default Permissions

`umask` sets the default permissions of new files as bits to be **removed** from the mode. With `umask` 0002, `> foo.txt` creates `-rw-rw-r--`: world loses write. In binary, mask `000 000 010 010` applied to `--- rw- rw- rw-` yields `--- rw- r-- r--`: every 1 in the mask unsets that attribute; `umask 0000` leaves the file world-writable. The default is usually fine; high-security situations control it.

## Some Special Permissions

A fourth octal digit carries three rare bits. The **setuid bit** (4000) on an executable changes the effective user ID to the program's owner, so setuid root programs run with superuser privileges and must be kept to a minimum. The **setgid bit** (2000) does the same for the group ID; on a directory, new files inherit the directory's group rather than the creator's. The **sticky bit** (1000), ignored on files, blocks deleting or renaming inside a directory unless you own the directory, own the file, or are the superuser (/tmp). Set them with `chmod u+s program`, `chmod g+s dir`, `chmod +t dir`, shown in `ls` as `-rwsr-xr-x`, `drwxrwsr-x`, `drwxrwxrwt`.

## Changing Identities

Three ways to become another user: log out and back in, `su`, or `sudo`. `su [-[l]] [user]` starts a shell as another user; `su -` loads the superuser's environment and home directory, marked by a trailing `#` prompt (`exit` returns); `su -c 'command'` runs one quoted command so expansion happens in the new shell. `sudo` runs commands under `/etc/sudoers` rules, authenticates with **your own password** and starts no new shell; `sudo -l` lists your privileges. Ubuntu disables root login entirely and relies on sudo; here you are already the superuser, so elevation is never needed.

## chown, chgrp, and a Shared Directory

`chown [owner][:[group]] file...` (superuser only) changes ownership: `bob` sets the owner, `bob:users` owner and group, `:admins` the group only, `bob:` the owner plus their login group. `chgrp` is the older group-only equivalent.

Setting up a shared directory for users bill and karen in group music (first four steps run through sudo on a normal system): `mkdir /usr/local/share/Music`, `chown :music`, `chmod 775`, `chmod g+s`, `umask 0002`. Group music plus 775 lets members write while others only list; umask 0022 would make new files `-rw-r--r--`, uneditable by the other members, and without setgid new files take the creator's primary group. Afterwards new files are `-rw-rw-r-- 1 bill music` and directories `drwxrwsr-x`; umask lasts only for the session.

## Changing Your Password

`passwd [user]` prompts for old and new passwords and enforces strong ones (`BAD PASSWORD: it is WAY too short`). The superuser may set other users' passwords and lock or expire accounts.

## Summary

- Every file has an owner, a group owner and the world, with read, write and execute rights; directories use x to enter and w (with x) to create and delete inside.
- `chmod` sets modes in octal or symbolically (u/g/o/a, +/−/=, r/w/x); `umask` removes bits from new files' default mode.
- setuid, setgid and the sticky bit form the fourth octal digit; `su`/`sudo` change identity, `chown`/`chgrp` ownership.
- The shared-directory recipe: group ownership, 775, setgid, umask 0002.

exercises.title: Set modes with octal and symbolic notation
exercises.instructions:
Create a file and change its mode two ways, exactly as the book does. Only the owner or the superuser can change a mode, and here you are the superuser—`id` shows uid=0:

```bash
mkdir -p /root/playground
cd /root/playground
touch secret.txt
ls -l secret.txt
chmod 600 secret.txt
ls -l secret.txt
chmod u+x,g-w,o-rwx secret.txt
ls -l secret.txt
id
```

Reasoning: `600` is `rw-------` (owner read/write only). The symbolic change then adds execute for the owner and strips everything from group and world, leaving `-rwx------`—the same result as `chmod 700`.
exercises.hint: Each octal digit is three permission bits: 7 is rwx, 6 rw-, 4 r--, 0 ---; `u+x` adds one attribute without disturbing the others.

verification_rules.feedback_on_failure: Run `mkdir -p /root/playground` and then `touch /root/playground/secret.txt`.
Run `chmod 700 /root/playground/secret.txt` to get owner rwx and no permissions for anyone else.
Run `id` to display your user identity; logged in as the superuser it shows uid=0.

exercises.title: Shape default permissions with umask
exercises.instructions:
The umask removes permission bits from the mode a new file is born with. Watch it work, as in the book:

```bash
cd /root/playground
rm -f umask_demo.txt private.txt
umask
umask 0022
touch umask_demo.txt
ls -l umask_demo.txt
umask 0077
touch private.txt
ls -l private.txt
umask 0022
```

With mask 0022 the new file is `-rw-r--r--` (world write is masked out); with 0077 it is `-rw-------`, readable and writable only by the owner. Restore 0022 when you are done—clean up like the book says.
exercises.hint: Expand the mask to binary: wherever a 1 bit appears, that permission is removed from the file's original mode.

verification_rules.feedback_on_failure: Set the mask first, then create the file: `umask 0022` followed by `touch /root/playground/umask_demo.txt`.
Set the mask first, then create the file: `umask 0077` followed by `touch /root/playground/private.txt`.

lessons.title: Chapter 10: Processes
lessons.description: You can explain how Linux organizes programs as parent and child processes with PIDs, move jobs between the foreground and background, and end processes with the kill and killall signals.
lessons.content:
# Chapter 10: Processes

Modern operating systems are multitasking: they create the illusion of doing several things at once by rapidly switching between programs. The kernel organizes these as **processes** waiting for their turn at the CPU. When a computer becomes sluggish or an application stops responding, `ps`, `top`, `jobs`, `bg`, `fg`, `kill`, `killall` and `shutdown` let us examine and terminate processes.

## How a Process Works

At startup the kernel launches `init`—always PID 1—which runs the **init scripts** in `/etc` that start the services; many are **daemons**: background programs with no user interface. A program launching another is a **parent process** producing a **child process**; processes, like files, have owners and user IDs.

## Viewing Processes with ps

```bash
[me@linuxbox ~]$ ps
  PID TTY           TIME CMD
 5198 pts/1    00:00:00 bash
10129 pts/1    00:00:00 ps
```

By default `ps` shows only the current terminal's processes; TTY ("teletype") is the controlling terminal, TIME the CPU time consumed. The `x` option (no leading dash) lists every process we own—`?` means no controlling terminal—and adds the `STAT` column:

| State | Meaning |
|---|---|
| R | Running, or ready to run. |
| S | Sleeping: waiting for an event such as a keystroke. |
| D | Uninterruptible sleep: waiting for I/O. |
| T | Stopped. |
| Z | Defunct or "zombie": a terminated child not cleaned up by its parent. |
| < | High-priority process; giving a process more CPU time is called **niceness**, so such a process is "less nice". |
| N | Low-priority process, served after higher-priority ones. |

The options `aux` (no leading dash, "BSD-style") show every user's processes with columns USER (owner), %CPU, %MEM, VSZ (virtual memory size), RSS (physical memory in kB) and START.

## Viewing Processes Dynamically with top

`ps` is a snapshot; `top` updates every three seconds by default, sorting processes by CPU activity under a system summary:

```
top - 14:59:20 up 6:30, 2 users, load average: 0.07, 0.02, 0.00
Tasks: 109 total,   1 running, 106 sleeping,   0 stopped,   2 zombie
Cpu(s): 0.7%us, 1.0%sy, 0.0%ni, 98.3%id, 0.0%wa, 0.0%hi, 0.0%si
Mem:    319496k total,   314860k used,     4636k free,    19392k buff
```

Row one gives the time, **uptime**, users and **load average**—runnable processes sharing the CPU over the last 1, 5 and 15 minutes; under 1.0 the machine is not busy. Tasks summarizes states; Cpu(s) splits work into user (us), kernel (sy), nice (ni), idle (id) and I/O wait (wa); Mem and Swap show memory use. `h` shows help, `q` quits; top is faster and lighter than graphical monitors, so the monitor itself does not cause the slowdown you are tracking.

## Controlling Processes: Job Control

The book's guinea pig is `xlogo`, a sample X Window program; `sleep` serves equally well. A running program holds the prompt until it finishes; **ctrl-C interrupts** it—a polite request to terminate. To keep the prompt, append an **ampersand** and the job runs in the **background**:

```bash
[me@linuxbox ~]$ xlogo &
[1] 28236
[me@linuxbox ~]$ jobs
[1]+ Running                    xlogo &
```

The shell reports job `[1]` with PID 28236—this is **job control**; `jobs` lists jobs launched from our terminal. Background jobs are immune to terminal input, so `fg %1`—a **jobspec**, optional with one job—returns one to the foreground. **ctrl-Z stops** (pauses) a foreground job (`[1]+ Stopped    xlogo`); `bg %1` resumes it in the background.

## Signals: Ending Processes with kill

`kill` does not exactly kill—it **sends signals**, the OS's way of communicating with programs. ctrl-C sends INT, ctrl-Z sends TSTP; programs listen and may act, say saving work first. Syntax: `kill -signal PID...`, default TERM; jobspecs replace PIDs, and you must own a process (or be the superuser) to signal it.

| Number | Name | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | HUP | Hang up: sent when a terminal session closes; many daemons reread their configuration on it. |
| 2 | INT | Interrupt: the ctrl-C equivalent. |
| 9 | KILL | Never delivered to the target—the kernel ends the process instantly, no cleanup; last resort only. |
| 15 | TERM | Terminate: kill's default. |
| 18 | CONT | Continue: restores a stopped process; sent by bg and fg. |
| 19 | STOP | Stop: pauses without terminating; cannot be ignored, like KILL. |
| 20 | TSTP | Terminal stop: the ctrl-Z signal; the program may ignore it. |

Signals may be numbered or named, with or without a SIG prefix (`kill -1`, `kill -INT`, `kill -SIGINT`); `kill -l` lists them. Others: 3 QUIT, 11 SEGV (illegal memory use), 28 WINCH (window change—top and less redraw). `killall [-u user] [-signal] name...` signals every process matching a program name.

## Shutting Down the System

Orderly shutdown terminates all processes and syncs mounted file systems. `halt`, `poweroff` and `reboot` act at once; `shutdown` picks action and delay (`shutdown -h now` halts, `shutdown -r now` reboots; use with sudo on a normal system) and warns logged-in users. Delayed execution with `at` and cron belongs to `/etc/crontab` and later chapters.

## More Process-Related Commands

`pstree` lists processes in a tree-like pattern showing parent-child relationships; `vmstat` snapshots memory, swap and disk I/O, and with a delay (`vmstat 5`) updates until ctrl-C; `xload`/`tload` graph system load.

## Summary

- Processes are how the kernel schedules programs; init (PID 1) starts the services and parents produce children.
- `ps` snapshots processes (`x`, `aux`); STAT covers running, sleeping, stopped, zombie and the niceness markers < and N.
- `top` updates continuously with uptime, load average, task states and CPU/memory/swap rows.
- Job control: `&` backgrounds, `jobs` lists, ctrl-C interrupts, ctrl-Z stops, and `bg`/`fg` resume with jobspecs.
- `kill`/`killall` send signals: TERM is the default; KILL is instant and unignorable, a last resort.
- Command line process tools beat GUI monitors for speed and light footprint.

exercises.title: Run and move jobs between foreground and background
exercises.instructions:
In the book, xlogo is the guinea pig; here `sleep` plays the same role. Launch a program so it is immediately placed in the background and watch the shell report the jobspec and PID:

```bash
mkdir -p /root/playground
sleep 30 &
jobs
echo background job started > /root/playground/bg.log
```

The `&` returns the prompt at once while the job runs in the background, and `jobs` lists it as Running. Now type `sleep 60`, press ctrl-Z to stop (pause) it, run `bg %1` to resume it in the background, and `jobs` again to see it there.
exercises.hint: A background job is immune to ctrl-C; use fg with its jobspec (for example %1) to bring it back to the foreground before interrupting it.

verification_rules.feedback_on_failure: Run `jobs` in the terminal to list jobs launched from this shell; start one with `sleep 30 &` if the list is empty.
Run `echo background job started > /root/playground/bg.log` to write the job log.

exercises.title: End a process with a signal
exercises.instructions:
`kill` doesn't literally kill—it sends signals. Launch a long-running job and note the PID the shell prints:

```bash
sleep 600 &
```

Replace 1234 below with the real PID from the shell's `[1] 1234` message and terminate the job:

```bash
kill 1234
echo terminated with TERM > /root/playground/kill.log
```

The default TERM signal lets the process clean up; KILL (signal 9) is never actually delivered—the kernel ends the process instantly—so the book says to use it only as a last resort. When the job dies the shell reports `[1]+ Terminated  sleep 600`. Also list every signal with `kill -l`.
exercises.hint: If a process ignores TERM, try `kill -9` with its PID—but KILL gives the process no chance to save its work.

verification_rules.feedback_on_failure: Run `echo terminated with TERM > /root/playground/kill.log` in the terminal.
Run `whoami`; as root you may send signals to every process on this system.

lessons.description: Read, set and export environment variables, and see how the bash startup files build your personal environment. After this lesson you can safely edit .bashrc to persist variables, history settings and aliases.
lessons.content:
# Chapter 11: The Environment

The shell maintains a body of information during a session called the **environment**. Programs use it to determine facts about the system's configuration, so we can use it to customize our shell experience. This chapter works with `printenv`, `set`, `export` and `alias`.

## Examining the Environment

The shell stores **environment variables** and **shell variables** (data placed there by bash), plus aliases and shell functions. The contents list is long, so pipe it into a pager:

```bash
[me@linuxbox ~]$ printenv | less
USER=me
PAGER=less
HOME=/home/me
```

`printenv USER` displays a single variable; `set` (without arguments) shows both shell and environment variables, sorted alphabetically, plus shell functions. Neither displays **aliases**; the `alias` command without arguments shows entries like `alias vi='vim'`.

## Some Interesting Variables

| Variable | Contents |
| --- | --- |
| DISPLAY | X display name, usually `:0` |
| EDITOR | The program used for text editing |
| SHELL | The name of your shell program |
| HOME | The pathname of your home directory |
| LANG | Character set and collation order of your language |
| OLDPWD | The previous working directory |
| PAGER | The program used for paging output |
| PATH | Colon-separated list of directories searched for command names |
| PS1 | "Prompt string 1" — defines the shell prompt |
| PWD | The current working directory |
| TERM | The name of your terminal type |
| TZ | Your time zone; the clock is kept in UTC |
| USER | Your username |

Missing values vary by distribution.

## How Is the Environment Established?

When we log on, bash reads **startup files**: global files defining the default environment shared by all users, then files in our home directory defining our personal environment. The sequence depends on the session type: a **login shell** (we are prompted for our username and password, e.g. a virtual console) or a **non-login shell** (a terminal session in the GUI).

| File | Read by |
| --- | --- |
| /etc/profile | Login shells — global script for all users |
| ~/.bash_profile | Login shells — personal startup file; can override global settings |
| ~/.bash_login | Login shells — if ~/.bash_profile is not found |
| ~/.profile | Login shells — if neither exists; the Debian-based default |
| /etc/bash.bashrc | Non-login shells — global script for all users |
| ~/.bashrc | Non-login shells — personal startup file |

Non-login shells also inherit the environment from their parent process, usually a login shell. `~/.bashrc` is the most important startup file for the ordinary user, because it is almost always read.

## What's in a Startup File?

A typical `.bash_profile` (from a CentOS 6 system):

```bash
# .bash_profile

# Get the aliases and functions
if [ -f ~/.bashrc ]; then
        . ~/.bashrc
fi

# User specific environment and startup programs

PATH=$PATH:$HOME/bin
export PATH
```

The `if` compound command reads ~/.bashrc if it exists. `PATH=$PATH:$HOME/bin` uses **parameter expansion**, appending to a variable's contents (as in `foo=$foo"text."`), so a `bin` directory in our home is searched for our own private programs. `export PATH` then makes the contents of PATH available to child processes of this shell. Ubuntu even adds `~/bin` to PATH automatically when the directory exists.

## Modifying the Environment

As a general rule, place PATH additions and new environment variables in `.bash_profile` (or your distribution's equivalent); everything else goes in `.bashrc`. Practice "safe computing" — back up before editing with `cp .bashrc .bashrc.bak`. Startup files are edited with a **text editor** — graphical (gedit, kate) or text-based (nano, vi, emacs). The chapter appends the following to `.bashrc` in nano (`ctrl-O` saves, `ctrl-X` exits):

```bash
umask 0002
export HISTCONTROL=ignoredups
export HISTSIZE=1000
alias l.='ls -d .* --color=auto'
alias ll='ls -l --color=auto'
```

These ease the shared-directory umask problem of Chapter 9, ignore history duplicates, grow the history to 1,000 lines, and create the `l.` and `ll` commands. Add `#` comments to document your changes — you won't remember them in six months. `.bashrc` is read only at the start of a session, so force bash to reread it:

```bash
[me@linuxbox ~]$ source ~/.bashrc
```

This course's guest terminal runs BusyBox `ash`, not bash; `export`, `env`, `alias` and `.bashrc` edits still work.

## Summary

- Editing configuration files with a text editor is an essential skill.
- `printenv`, `set` and `alias` reveal what the environment stores.
- Login shells read `/etc/profile` and `~/.bash_profile` (or `~/.profile`); non-login shells read `~/.bashrc`.
- Parameter expansion extends `PATH`; `export` hands variables to child processes.
- Back up files before editing, comment your changes, and activate with `source ~/.bashrc`.
- As we read man pages, note the environment variables commands support — there may be a gem or two.

lessons.content:
# Chapter 12: A Gentle Introduction to vi

**vi** (pronounced "vee eye") is one of the core programs in the Unix tradition, notorious for its difficult user interface. This chapter gets us to the equivalent of "Chopsticks" in vi: the editing modes, moving, inserting, deleting, cutting and pasting, searching, replacing, and multiple files.

## Why We Should Learn vi

- vi is almost always available — POSIX requires it — a lifesaver on a system with no graphical interface.
- vi is lightweight, fast, and designed for typing speed: a skilled user never lifts their fingers from the keyboard.
- We don't want other Linux and Unix users to think we are cowards.

Bill Joy wrote the first vi in 1976; the name means "visual" — editing with a moving cursor, unlike the earlier **line editors**. vi incorporates a line editor called **ex**, whose commands we can use. Most distributions ship **vim** ("vi improved"), by Bram Moolenaar, linked or aliased to `vi`.

## Starting and Stopping vi

Start with `vi`, or pass a nonexistent filename to create a new file:

```bash
[me@linuxbox ~]$ vi foo.txt
```

Exit with the ex command `:q` (the colon is part of the command); if it refuses because of unsaved changes, show you really mean it with `:q!`. If you get "lost" in vi, press the `esc` key twice. If vim reports "Running in Vi compatible mode," add a line to your vim configuration file:

```bash
echo "set nocp" >> ~/.vimrc
```

## Editing Modes

The second most important thing to learn is that vi is a **modal editor**. It starts in **command mode**, where almost every key is a command — typing text directly makes a big mess. Press `i` to enter **insert mode** (`-- INSERT --` appears at the bottom) and type the book's example line:

```
The quick brown fox jumped over the lazy dog.
```

Press `esc`, then `:` and `w` to write the file; vi confirms with `"foo.txt" [New] 1L, 46C written`.

## Moving the Cursor

| Key | Moves the cursor |
| --- | --- |
| h / l (or arrows) | Left / right one character |
| j / k (or arrows) | Down / up one line |
| 0 / ^ / $ | Line start / first non-blank / line end |
| w / b | Next / previous word or punctuation (W / B ignores punctuation) |
| ctrl-F / ctrl-B | Down / up one page |
| numberG / G | To line number / to the last line |

h, j, k, l were chosen because early terminals had no arrow keys. Many commands take a numeric prefix: `5j` moves down five lines.

## Inserting and Deleting Text

- `a` appends after the cursor; `A` moves to the line end first.
- `o` opens a blank line below in insert mode; `O` opens one above.
- `x` deletes the character; `3x` deletes three.
- `d` plus a movement command deletes that span: `dd` the current line, `5dd` five lines, `d$` to the line end, `dG` to the end of the file.
- `u` undoes the last change (real vi has one undo level; vim has many).

`d` also "cuts": deletions go into a paste buffer (think clipboard) recalled with `p` (paste after the cursor) or `P` (before). `y` "yanks" (copies) using all the movement commands `d` does: `yy` copies the current line.

## Searching and Search-and-Replace

- `fa` moves to the next `a` within the current line; repeat with `;`.
- `/Line` jumps to the next occurrence in the file, as in `less`; `n` repeats. Regular expressions are allowed.
- Global search-and-replace is an ex **substitution**:

```
:%s/Line/line/g
```

| Item | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| : | Starts an ex command |
| % | Line range, first to last (omitted = current line) |
| s | The operation: substitution |
| /Line/line/ | Search pattern and replacement text |
| g | Every instance on the line; omitted, only the first per line |

Adding `c` requires confirmation — `:%s/line/Line/gc` asks `replace with Line (y/n/a/q/l/^E/^Y)?`: y substitutes, n skips, a does the rest, q or esc quits, l ("last") substitutes and quits.

## Editing Multiple Files

```bash
[me@linuxbox ~]$ ls -l /usr/bin > ls-output.txt
[me@linuxbox ~]$ vi foo.txt ls-output.txt
```

- `:bn` and `:bp` switch to the next / previous file; vi refuses if there are unsaved changes — add `!` to force it.
- `:buffers` lists open files, `:buffer 2` jumps to buffer 2, `:e file` adds one.
- Copy between files: `yy` a line in one buffer, `:buffer 2`, then `p`.
- `:r foo.txt` ("read") inserts an entire file below the cursor position.

## Saving Our Work

`:w` writes; `:wq` (or `ZZ` in command mode) saves and exits; `:q!` abandons changes. `:w foo1.txt` acts like Save As — though you are still editing `foo.txt`.

## Summary

- vi is a modal editor: `i` inserts, `esc` returns to command mode, `:w` writes, `:q`/`:q!` quit, `:wq` or `ZZ` saves and exits.
- Movement keys (h j k l, w, b, $, G) with numeric prefixes keep the fingers on the keyboard.
- `d` cuts, `y` yanks, `p`/`P` paste, `o`/`O` open lines, `u` undoes.
- `/` searches; `:%s/old/new/g` replaces globally, `c` confirms each change.
- Multiple files: `:bn`, `:bp`, `:buffers`, `:e`, `:r`; vi-style design (even in `less`) rewards practice.

lessons.description: Control PS1 with backslash escape sequences, ANSI colour codes and cursor movement, and make prompt customisations permanent in .bashrc. After this lesson you can back up the current prompt and persist a timestamped prompt plus an alias.
lessons.content:
# Chapter 13: Customizing the Prompt

This chapter looks at a seemingly trivial detail — our shell prompt — revealing inner workings of the shell and terminal emulator. Our default prompt looks like this:

```
[me@linuxbox ~]$
```

It contains our username, hostname and current working directory — a really useful device once we learn to control it.

## Anatomy of a Prompt: PS1

The prompt is defined by an environment variable named **PS1** (short for "prompt string 1"):

```bash
[me@linuxbox ~]$ echo $PS1
[\u@\h \W]\$
```

Besides the brackets, at-sign and dollar sign, PS1 holds backslash-escaped special characters that bash treats specially in the prompt string. Don't worry if your results differ — every distribution defines the prompt string a little differently.

## Escape Sequences and Special Characters

| Sequence | Value displayed |
| --- | --- |
| \a | ASCII bell — the computer beeps |
| \d / \j / \l / \s | Date / job count / terminal device / shell name |
| \h / \H | Hostname minus / including trailing domain |
| \t / \T / \@ / \A | Time: 24-hour, 12-hour, am/pm, hh:mm |
| \u | Username of the current user |
| \v / \V | Shell version / release |
| \w / \W | Full working directory / its last part |
| \! / \# | History number / commands entered |
| \$ | `$`, or `#` if we have superuser privileges |
| \[ and \] | Start and end of non-printing characters |

First back up the prompt string: `ps1_old="$PS1"`, then restore it later with `PS1="$ps1_old"`. An empty string gives no prompt at all; a minimal prompt is `PS1="\$ "` — the trailing space keeps the cursor off the dollar sign. A bell (`PS1="\[\a\]\$ "`) needs the `\[...\]` wrappers: `\a` does not move the cursor and bash must determine the prompt's true length. Time-of-day tracks when we perform tasks:

```bash
$ PS1="\A \h \$ "
17:33 linuxbox $
$ PS1="<\u@\h \W>\$ "
<me@linuxbox ~>$
```

## Adding Color

Terminal emulators respond to **ANSI escape codes**. A code begins with octal 033 (the esc key), an optional attribute, then an instruction: `\033[0;30m` is normal (attribute 0) black text.

| Sequence | Text color | Sequence | Text color |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| \033[0;30m | Black | \033[1;30m | Dark gray |
| \033[0;31m | Red | \033[1;31m | Light red |
| \033[0;32m | Green | \033[1;32m | Light green |
| \033[0;33m | Brown | \033[1;33m | Yellow |
| \033[0;34m | Blue | \033[1;34m | Light blue |
| \033[0;35m | Purple | \033[1;35m | Light purple |
| \033[0;36m | Cyan | \033[1;36m | Light cyan |
| \033[0;37m | Light gray | \033[1;37m | White |

The bold attribute (1) creates "light" colors. Insert the code at the start of the prompt:

```bash
<me@linuxbox ~>$ PS1="\[\033[0;31m\]<\u@\h \W>\$ "
```

Now everything we type is red too, so append a reset code returning to the previous color: `PS1="\[\033[0;31m\]<\u@\h \W>\$\[\033[0m\] "`. Backgrounds use `\033[0;40m`-`\033[0;47m` (black through light gray), no bold; underscore (4), blinking (5) and inverse (7) attributes also exist.

## Moving the Cursor

Escape codes position the cursor: `\033[l;cH` moves to line l, column c; `\033[nA`/`\033[nB` move up/down n lines; `\033[nC`/`\033[nD` move forward/back n characters; `\033[2J` clears the screen; `\033[K` clears to the line end; `\033[s`/`\033[u` store and recall the position. The book draws a red bar with a yellow clock at the top of the screen each time the prompt appears:

```bash
PS1="\[\033[s\033[0;0H\033[0;41m\033[K\033[1;33m\t\033[0m\033[u\]<\u@\h \W>\$ "
```

It stores the cursor, jumps to the upper-left corner, paints the red bar with `\033[K`, prints the time in yellow, resets color, restores the cursor, then draws `<\u@\h \W>$`. Wrapping it in `\[...\]` matters: without an accurate size calculation for the visible prompt, command line editing cannot position the cursor correctly.

## Saving the Prompt

To stop typing that monster, make the prompt permanent by adding these lines to `.bashrc`:

```bash
PS1="\[\033[s\033[0;0H\033[0;41m\033[K\033[1;33m\t\033[0m\033[u\]<\u@\h \W>\$ "
export PS1
```

Beyond the chapter: bash also defines **PS2**, the continuation prompt for incomplete commands, and `\$?` in PS1 shows the previous command's exit status when the prompt draws. Aliases (Chapter 11) live in this same `.bashrc`. The guest's BusyBox `ash` won't interpret bash's `\u`-style escapes, but assignment, export and `.bashrc` edits all work.

## Summary

- The prompt's contents come from PS1; view it with `echo $PS1` and back it up with `ps1_old="$PS1"`.
- Escape sequences (\u, \h, \W, \t, \A, \$) insert username, hostname, directory and time-of-day values.
- Non-printing characters must be wrapped in `\[` and `\]` so bash calculates the prompt's length.
- ANSI codes `\033[...m` set text and background colors; `\033[0m` restores the previous color.
- Cursor codes (\033[s, \033[0;0H, \033[K, \033[u) allow extras like a timestamped clock bar.
- Save a customized prompt by assigning PS1 and exporting it in `.bashrc`.

lessons.title: Chapter 14: Package Management
lessons.description: Explain how package files, repositories, dependencies and low/high-level tools (dpkg and apt on Debian-style systems, rpm and yum on Red Hat-style systems) fit together, and take a software inventory of a live system from the command line.
lessons.content:
# Chapter 14: Package Management

Package management is a method of installing and maintaining software on the system. Because most top-tier distributions release new versions every six months and many program updates every day, we need good tools to keep up; the packaging system is the most important determinant of distribution quality. While distributions provide graphical programs, the command line tools can perform many tasks that are difficult or impossible with their graphical counterparts.

## Packaging Systems

Different distributions use different packaging systems, and a package for one distribution is generally not compatible with another. Most fall into two camps:

| Packaging system | Distributions (partial listing) |
| --- | --- |
| Debian-style (.deb) | Debian, Ubuntu, Linux Mint, Raspbian |
| Red Hat-style (.rpm) | Fedora, CentOS, Red Hat Enterprise Linux, OpenSUSE |

## How a Package System Works

The basic unit is the **package file**: a compressed collection of files comprising the software, plus **metadata** (a text description of the package) and often pre- and post-installation scripts. A **package maintainer** gets software in source code form from the upstream provider, compiles it, and creates the metadata and scripts.

Packages live in central **repositories** — a "testing" repository, a "development" repository, and third-party repositories for software that cannot legally be included with the distribution. Since programs rely on shared libraries, a package **has a dependency**; package systems perform dependency resolution so dependencies get installed too.

Systems offer **low-level tools** (install and remove package files) and **high-level tools** (metadata searching and dependency resolution):

| Distributions | Low-level tools | High-level tools |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Debian-style | dpkg | apt-get, apt, aptitude |
| Fedora, RHEL, CentOS | rpm | yum, dnf |

## Common Package Management Tasks

Here `package_name` is the name of a package; `package_file` is the file that contains it.

| Task | Debian-style | Red Hat-style |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Search the repository | `apt-get update; apt-cache search search_string` | `yum search search_string` |
| Install from a repository | `apt-get install package_name` | `yum install package_name` |
| Install a package file | `dpkg -i package_file` | `rpm -i package_file` |
| Remove a package | `apt-get remove package_name` | `yum erase package_name` |
| Update all packages | `apt-get update; apt-get upgrade` | `yum update` |
| Upgrade from a file | `dpkg -i package_file` | `rpm -U package_file` |
| List installed packages | `dpkg -l` | `rpm -qa` |
| Package status | `dpkg -s package_name` | `rpm -q package_name` |
| Package information | `apt-cache show package_name` | `yum info package_name` |
| Which package owns a file | `dpkg -S file_name` | `rpm -qf file_name` |

```bash
yum search emacs
apt-get update; apt-get install emacs
rpm -qf /usr/bin/vim
```

> **Note:** Low-level installation of a package file (`rpm -i emacs-22.1-7.fc7-i386.rpm`) performs no dependency resolution; rpm exits with an error on a missing dependency. dpkg has no specific upgrade option as rpm does.

## Source Packages

Nothing is wrong with compiling source code — access to source is the great wonder of Linux, letting us examine and improve the system; a precompiled package is just faster and easier. Device drivers become part of the Linux kernel, so there is no such thing as a "driver disk": either the kernel supports a device or it doesn't. Missing support usually means the device is too new, too exotic, or the vendor is hiding something — products best avoided.

## Summary

- Most distributions use the Debian .deb or Red Hat .rpm packaging family; packages are not interchangeable.
- Package files bundle programs, data, metadata and install scripts; repositories distribute them and dependency resolution installs required shared libraries.
- Low-level tools (dpkg, rpm) install and remove files; high-level tools (apt-get, apt-cache, yum, dnf) search metadata and resolve dependencies.
- Common tasks: search, install, remove, update, list, query status, show information, and find which package installed a file.
- Compiling from source is powerful but slower than packages; drivers live in the kernel, so Linux has no driver disks.
