lessons.description: Write your first shell script with a shebang, make it executable with chmod, and place it where the shell's PATH can find it. You will also learn the formatting tricks that keep scripts readable and maintainable.
lessons.content:
# Chapter 24: Writing Your First Script

A shell script is a plain text file containing a series of commands that the shell executes as if they had been entered directly on the command line. This first scripting chapter shows how to write a script, give it a shebang, make it executable, and place it where the shell can find it, plus formatting tricks that keep scripts maintainable.

## What Are Shell Scripts?

The shell is both a command line interface and a scripting language interpreter. Most things that can be done on the command line can be done in scripts, and vice versa. By joining command line tools into programs of our own design, the shell can carry out complex sequences of tasks all by itself.

## How to Write a Shell Script

Three things are required: write the script in a text editor (vim, gedit, kate and friends provide syntax highlighting that helps spot common errors), make the script **executable** by setting its permissions, and put the script somewhere the shell can find it.

## Script File Format

Following programming tradition, the book's first script is a "Hello World" program, saved as `hello_world`:

```bash
#!/bin/bash

# This is our first script.

echo 'Hello World!'
```

The first line is a special construct called a **shebang**: the `#!` sequence tells the kernel which interpreter should execute the script that follows, so every shell script should include it as its first line. Everything after a `#` on a line is a comment, and comments may also appear at the ends of lines:

```
[me@linuxbox ~]$ echo 'Hello World!' # This is a comment too
Hello World!
```

Because the kernel launches the interpreter named in the shebang, running a script directly honors the shebang, while invoking it as `sh hello_world` deliberately runs the plain POSIX `sh` instead. Feature sets differ between shells: bash-only syntax such as `[[ ]]` does not work in `sh`, and on the practice VM (BusyBox `ash`) write `#!/bin/sh` and stick to POSIX syntax, since bash may not be installed.

## Executable Permissions

The system is fussy about not letting any old text file be treated as a program, so we must set execution permission with chmod:

```
[me@linuxbox ~]$ ls -l hello_world
-rw-r--r-- 1 me      me      63 2018-03-07 10:10 hello_world
[me@linuxbox ~]$ chmod 755 hello_world
-rwxr-xr-x 1 me      me      63 2018-03-07 10:10 hello_world
```

The two common settings are **755** for scripts everyone can execute and **700** for scripts only the owner can execute. Scripts must be readable to be executed.

## Script File Location

A script only runs when reached through a path:

```
[me@linuxbox ~]$ ./hello_world
Hello World!
[me@linuxbox ~]$ hello_world
bash: hello_world: command not found
```

The **PATH** variable holds a colon-separated list of directories the shell searches for executables, typically including `~/bin`. Create it and move the script in, and it starts working like any other program:

```
[me@linuxbox ~]$ mkdir bin
[me@linuxbox ~]$ mv hello_world bin
[me@linuxbox ~]$ hello_world
Hello World!
```

If your PATH lacks it, add this line to `.bashrc` and re-source the file with the dot command (`. .bashrc`, a synonym for `source`):

```bash
export PATH=~/bin:"$PATH"
```

Good locations: `~/bin` for personal scripts, `/usr/local/bin` for scripts everyone may use, `/usr/local/sbin` for administrator scripts; `/bin` and `/usr/bin` are reserved for files supplied by the distributor.

## More Formatting Tricks

The key goal of serious script writing is ease of maintenance. Prefer long option names in scripts (`ls --all --directory` rather than `ls -ad`) and spread long commands over several lines with continuations (backslash-linefeed) and indentation:

```bash
find playground \
      \( \
            -type f \
            -not -perm 0600 \
            -exec chmod 0600 '{}' ';' \
      \) \
      -or \
      \( \
            -type d \
            -not -perm 0700 \
            -exec chmod 0700 '{}' ';' \
      \)
```

Scripts may use tab characters for indentation, unlike the command line where tabs trigger completion.

## Summary

- A shell script is a text file of commands the shell runs in sequence.
- The shebang (`#!`) on the first line tells the kernel which interpreter executes the script.
- chmod 755 (or 700) makes a script executable; scripts must be readable to run.
- Scripts named without a path are found via PATH; keep personal scripts in `~/bin` and shared ones in `/usr/local/bin`.
- Comments, long options, indentation, and line continuation improve readability.
- Ease of maintenance is a central principle of good script writing.

exercises.title: Create the hello script
exercises.instructions:
Create `/root/hello.sh` containing the book's first script, adapted with a POSIX shebang because the practice VM's shell is BusyBox `ash`, and make it executable:

```bash

lessons.title: Chapter 25: Starting a Project
lessons.description: Start the book's report-generator project by outputting a minimal HTML page from a script, using variables and constants, command substitution, and here documents to shape the output.
lessons.content:
# Chapter 25: Starting a Project Starting with this chapter we build a program stage by stage: a report generator that presents statistics about our system and produces the report in HTML format. Along the way the chapter introduces **variables and constants**, assignment via expansions, and **here documents** as a way of producing output. ## First Stage: Minimal Document The first stage outputs a minimal well-formed HTML document to standard output. Create the file `~/bin/sys_info_page`: ```bash #!/bin/bash # Program to output a system information page echo "" echo " " echo " Page Title" echo " " echo " " echo " Page body." echo " " echo "" ``` Make it executable with `chmod 755`, and redirect its output to a file you can view in a browser: ``` [me@linuxbox ~]$ sys_info_page > sys_info_page.html ``` Because a quoted string may contain newlines, all the echo commands can be combined into one multiline command; the `>` continuation prompt the shell shows while you type it is the PS2 prompt: ```bash #!/bin/bash # Program to output a system information page echo " Page Title Page body. " ``` ## Variables and Constants The string "System Information Report" will appear many times, so store it once in a variable. The shell creates variables automatically when it encounters them, which means a misspelled name silently yields an empty string: ``` [me@linuxbox ~]$ foo="yes" [me@linuxbox ~]$ echo $fool [me@linuxbox ~]$ ``` An empty expansion can even break commands that require arguments (`cp $foo $fool` fails with "missing destination file operand"), so pay close attention to spelling. Variable names may contain letters, digits, and underscores, must begin with a letter or underscore, and may not contain spaces or punctuation. A **constant** uses the same syntax but is intended to keep one value; the convention is uppercase names for constants and lowercase for true variables: ```bash #!/bin/bash # Program to output a system information page TITLE="System Information Report For $HOSTNAME" echo " $TITLE

$TITLE

" ``` The shell makes no distinction between variables and constants; `declare -r TITLE="Page Title"` can enforce immutability for very formal scripts, but it is rarely used. ## Assigning Values to Variables and Constants Assignment is `variable=value` with no spaces around the equals sign, and the shell treats all data as strings. A value may be anything that expands into a string, including **command substitution** and arithmetic expansion: ```bash a=z # Assign the string "z" to variable a. b="a string" # Embedded spaces must be within quotes. c="a string and $b" # Other expansions can be expanded into the assignment. d="$(ls -l foo.txt)" # Results of a command. e=$((5 * 7)) # Arithmetic expansion. f="\t\ta string\n" # Escape sequences such as tabs and newlines. ``` Braces resolve ambiguous names — `mv "$filename" "${filename}1"` — and it is good practice to enclose variables and command substitutions in double quotes to limit word splitting. Adding real data to the report: ```bash TITLE="System Information Report For $HOSTNAME" CURRENT_TIME="$(date +"%x %r %Z")" TIMESTAMP="Generated $CURRENT_TIME, by $USER" ``` ## Here Documents A **here document** is a form of I/O redirection, `command << token`, in which we embed a body of text into a command's standard input until the token appears again on a line by itself. The report script now uses cat instead of echo: ```bash cat << _EOF_ $TITLE

$TITLE

$TIMESTAMP

_EOF_ ``` The token (`_EOF_`, "end of file", is the convention) must appear alone with no trailing spaces. Inside here documents, single and double quotes lose their special meaning, so quotes can be embedded freely: ``` [me@linuxbox ~]$ foo="some text" [me@linuxbox ~]$ cat << _EOF_ > $foo > "$foo" > '$foo' > \$foo > _EOF_ some text "some text" 'some text' $foo ``` Changing the redirection operator to `<<-` makes the shell ignore leading **tab** characters (not spaces), allowing an indented here document. ## Summary - Programs are built in stages; this chapter started the `sys_info_page` report generator. - Quoted strings can span lines, and here documents embed blocks of text into a command's standard input. - The shell creates variables on demand, so misspelled names expand to nothing and must be watched for. - Assignments accept any string, including results of command substitution $( ) and arithmetic expansion $(( )). - Uppercase names conventionally mark constants; `declare -r` can make one read-only. - Quoting variables and command substitutions protects against word splitting.

lessons.title: Chapter 26: Top-Down Design
lessons.description: Design a program top-down by decomposing it into shell functions, keep it runnable with stub functions and feedback, and use local variables so functions stay independent and reusable.
lessons.content:
# Chapter 26: Top-Down Design As programs grow larger and more complex, they become more difficult to design, code, and maintain. **Top-down design** breaks a large, complex task into a series of small, simple ones: describing "go to the market" at the top level (get in car, drive to market, park car, enter market, purchase food) and then decomposing each step further ("park car" becomes find parking space, drive in, turn off motor, set brake, exit, lock). This chapter applies that process, and **shell functions**, to our `sys_info_page` report generator. ## Shell Functions Shell functions are "mini-scripts" located inside other scripts that can act as autonomous programs. They have two equivalent syntactic forms: ```bash function name { commands return } ``` and the simpler, generally preferred form: ```bash name () { commands return } ``` A demonstration script: ```bash #!/bin/bash # Shell function demo function step2 { echo "Step 2" return } # Main program starts here echo "Step 1" step2 echo "Step 3" ``` The shell passes over the definition and begins executing at `echo "Step 1"`; calling `step2` runs the function, and `return` terminates it and hands control back to the line after the call. For function calls to be recognized as functions and not external programs, definitions must appear before they are called, and a function must contain at least one command. ## Stepwise Refinement of the Report The report needs three new sections: system uptime and load, disk space, and home space. We embed them as three functions whose output is injected into the here document by **command substitution** — `$(report_uptime)`, `$(report_disk_space)`, `$(report_home_space)` — between the heading and the closing body tag. First we add empty functions, called **stubs**, so the script stays runnable: ```bash report_uptime () { return } report_disk_space () { return } report_home_space () { return } ``` ## Local Variables All the variables so far have been global. A **local variable**, created with the `local` keyword inside a function, is accessible only within that function and ceases to exist when the function terminates, so functions can share names without conflicts and be cut and pasted between scripts: ```bash #!/bin/bash # local-vars: script to demonstrate local variables foo=0 # global variable foo funct_1 () { local foo # variable foo local to funct_1 foo=1 echo "funct_1: foo = $foo" } funct_2 () { local foo # variable foo local to funct_2 foo=2 echo "funct_2: foo = $foo" } echo "global: foo = $foo" funct_1 echo "global: foo = $foo" funct_2 echo "global: foo = $foo" ``` Running it shows the assignments inside the functions never disturb the global `foo`, which stays 0 throughout. ## Keep Scripts Running By keeping the program in a runnable state and testing frequently, errors are detected early: if the program ran fine before the most recent change, that change is the likely culprit. Giving each stub feedback proves the logical flow is carried out: ```bash report_uptime () { echo "Function report_uptime executed." return } ``` and the output of the script then lists the three "Function ... executed." lines after the timestamp. ## Fleshing Out the Functions With the framework verified, each function becomes a here document wrapping a command in `
` tags to preserve its formatting:

```bash
report_uptime () {
      cat <<- _EOF_
              
System Uptime

              
$(uptime)

              _EOF_
      return
}

report_disk_space () {
      cat <<- _EOF_
             
Disk Space Utilization

             
$(df -h)

             _EOF_
      return
}

report_home_space () {
      cat <<- _EOF_
             
Home Space Utilization

             
$(du -sh /home/*)

             _EOF_
      return
}
```

`uptime` reports time since boot and average processor load, `df -h` summarizes disk usage, and `du -sh /home/*` shows the space used by each user. The last is not a complete solution: many systems make home directories non-world-readable, so it only works fully with superuser privileges. Making the script adapt to the user's privileges is the job of the next chapter. Shell functions also make excellent, more capable replacements for aliases in `.bashrc` — for instance a `ds ()` function that echoes a heading and runs `df -h`.

## Summary

- Top-down design decomposes complex tasks into many small, simple ones, refined step by step.
- Shell functions are mini-scripts inside a script; definitions must appear before the calls.
- Command substitution lets functions inject their output into the here document.
- Stub functions with feedback keep scripts runnable so logical flow can be verified early.
- Local variables make functions independent of each other and of the enclosing script, which makes them portable and reusable.

lessons.title: Chapter 27: Flow Control: Branching with if
lessons.description: Branch your scripts with if/then/elif/else, evaluate file, string, and integer conditions with the test command and exit status, and combine expressions with the && and || control operators.
lessons.content:
# Chapter 27: Flow Control: Branching with if To make a script change directions based on a test — to branch — we need the `if` compound command and exit status, the `test`/`[ ]` command with its file, string, and integer expressions, the bash extensions `[[ ]]` and `(( ))`, and the `&&`/`||` control operators. ## if Statements The pseudocode logic "If X equals 5, say so; otherwise say otherwise" becomes: ```bash x=5 if [ "$x" -eq 5 ]; then echo "x equals 5." else echo "x does not equal 5." fi ``` The full syntax is `if commands; then commands [elif commands; then commands...] [else commands] fi`: `if` evaluates the success or failure of the commands after it. ## Exit Status Commands, including our scripts and functions, issue an **exit status** between 0 and 255 when they terminate; by convention zero indicates success and any other value failure. The parameter `$?` displays it: ``` [me@linuxbox ~]$ ls -d /bin/usr ls: cannot access /bin/usr: No such file or directory [me@linuxbox ~]$ echo $? 2 ``` The builtins `true` and `false` do nothing except terminate with status 0 and 1; when a list of commands follows `if`, the last one decides. ## Using test: File Expressions The command used most with `if` is `test`, in two equivalent forms, `test expression` and `[ expression ]`; it returns 0 when the expression is true. Useful file expressions: `-e` exists, `-f` regular file, `-d` directory, `-r`, `-w`, `-x` readable/writable/executable, `-s` non-empty, `-L` symlink. The book's demonstration script nests several tests: ```bash #!/bin/bash # test-file: Evaluate the status of a file FILE=~/.bashrc if [ -e "$FILE" ]; then if [ -f "$FILE" ]; then echo "$FILE is a regular file." fi if [ -d "$FILE" ]; then echo "$FILE is a directory." fi if [ -r "$FILE" ]; then echo "$FILE is readable." fi if [ -w "$FILE" ]; then echo "$FILE is writable." fi if [ -x "$FILE" ]; then echo "$FILE is executable/searchable." fi else echo "$FILE does not exist" exit 1 fi exit ``` `$FILE` is quoted inside every test — a defense against an empty expansion turning operators into strings — and `exit 1` reports failure. ## String and Integer Expressions String expressions: `string` (not null), `-n`, `-z`, `=`, `!=`, and `>`/`<` (quote them under `test` or they become redirections). Integer expressions: `-eq`, `-ne`, `-le`, `-lt`, `-ge`, `-gt`. The book's string script screens empty input to standard error and chains `elif` ("else if") branches: ```bash #!/bin/bash # test-string: evaluate the value of a string ANSWER=maybe if [ -z "$ANSWER" ]; then echo "There is no answer." >&2 exit 1 fi if [ "$ANSWER" = "yes" ]; then echo "The answer is YES." elif [ "$ANSWER" = "no" ]; then echo "The answer is NO." elif [ "$ANSWER" = "maybe" ]; then echo "The answer is MAYBE." else echo "The answer is UNKNOWN." fi ``` The integer script nests `if` inside `else` and finds even/odd with a modulo: `[ $((INT % 2)) -eq 0 ]`. ## A More Modern Version of test `[[ expression ]]` supports all of `test`'s expressions plus regular-expression matching, letting the integer script verify its value is really an integer: ```bash if [[ "$INT" =~ ^-?[0-9]+$ ]]; then ``` `[[ ]]` also supports pattern matching with `==` (`[[ $FILE == foo.* ]]`), and `(( ))` performs integer truth tests with natural syntax (`((INT < 0))`). Both are bash-only; `[ ]` is POSIX, which is what the BusyBox `ash` practice VM understands. ## Combining Expressions Logical operators join expressions: `-a`/`-o`/`!` for `test`, `&&`/`||`/`!` for `[[ ]]` and `(( ))`: ```bash if [[ "$INT" -ge "$MIN_VAL" && "$INT" -le "$MAX_VAL" ]]; then echo "$INT is within $MIN_VAL to $MAX_VAL." else echo "$INT is out of range." fi ``` `!` negates an expression, with parentheses grouping the combination; under `test` the parentheses must be escaped: `[ ! \( "$INT" -ge "$MIN_VAL" -a "$INT" -le "$MAX_VAL" \) ]`. ## Control Operators `command1 && command2` executes `command2` only if `command1` succeeds; `command1 || command2` only if it fails: ``` [me@linuxbox ~]$ mkdir temp && cd temp [me@linuxbox ~]$ [ -d temp ] || mkdir temp ``` This handles errors in scripts, for example `[ -d temp ] || exit 1`. ## Solving the Home Space Problem `id -u` outputs the effective user's numeric ID and the superuser is always zero, so the report script can adapt to its user: ```bash report_home_space () { if [[ "$(id -u)" -eq 0 ]]; then cat <<- _EOF_

Home Space Utilization (All Users)

$(du -sh /home/*)
_EOF_ else cat <<- _EOF_

Home Space Utilization ($USER)

$(du -sh $HOME)
_EOF_ fi return } ``` ## Summary - `if` branches on the exit status of commands; zero means success, and `$?` reveals the last status. - `test`/`[ ]` supplies file, string, and integer expressions; quote parameters and escape `<`, `>`, `(`, `)`. - `elif` builds multi-way branches, and error messages belong on standard error. - `[[ ]]` adds regex (`=~`) and pattern matching, and `(( ))` handles integer comparisons; both are bash-only. - The `&&` and `||` control operators branch on one command's success or failure.

lessons.title: Chapter 28: Reading Keyboard Input
lessons.description: Make scripts interactive with the read command and its prompt, silent, and timeout options, validate user input, and assemble a menu-driven program from the tools of the previous chapters.
lessons.content:
# Chapter 28: Reading Keyboard Input

Our scripts so far lack interactivity. The `read` builtin reads one line of standard input — from the keyboard or, with redirection, from a file — and this chapter combines it with branching to validate input and build menus.

## read

The syntax is `read [-options] [variable...]`; fields are assigned to the named variables, and with no names the whole line goes into `REPLY`. Making the integer evaluator interactive:

```bash
#!/bin/bash

# read-integer: evaluate the value of an integer.

echo -n "Please enter an integer -> "
read int
```

`echo -n` prints the prompt without a newline; the rest is the Chapter 27 validation plus the even/odd test `[ $((int % 2)) -eq 0 ]` built on the arithmetic expansion from Chapter 25 (the book treats arithmetic evaluation, including bash's `let`, later). With several names, missing inputs leave the extra variables empty and excess input piles into the last one (the book's read-multiple demo puts `'e f g'` in var5).

## Options

Options: `-p prompt`, `-n num` characters instead of a line, `-s` silent (for passwords), `-t seconds` timeout (non-zero exit status on timeout), `-r` raw, `-a array`, `-d delimiter`, `-u fd`, and bash's `-e`/`-i` Readline editing with a default reply. On the BusyBox `ash` VM `-p`, `-s`, `-n`, `-t` work; `-e`/`-i` are bash-only. The book combines `-t` and `-s`:

```bash
#!/bin/bash

# read-secret: input a secret passphrase

if read -t 10 -sp "Enter secret passphrase > " secret_pass; then
      echo -e "\nSecret passphrase = '$secret_pass'"
else
      echo -e "\nInput timed out" >&2
      exit 1
fi
```

## IFS and Here Strings

Read word-splits input using the `IFS` (Internal Field Separator) variable, by default space, tab, and newline. Setting `IFS=":"` parses `/etc/passwd` records, and the `<<<` **here string** feeds one string to a command's standard input:

```bash
IFS=":" read user pw uid gid name home shell <<< "$file_info"
```

The line combines a prefix assignment (alters the environment for that command only), the list of names, and a here string holding the line fetched by `file_info="$(grep "^$user_name:" $FILE)"`.

You cannot pipe `read`: `echo "foo" | read` appears to succeed but `REPLY` stays empty, because pipelines run in a **subshell** — a copy of the environment destroyed when the command finishes, so a subshell can never alter its parent's environment. Here strings are one workaround.

## Validating Input

The unexpected usually arrives as bad input, so every program should screen it. The book's validator combines shell functions, `[[ ]]`, `(( ))`, `&&`, and regular expressions:

```bash
#!/bin/bash

# read-validate: validate input

invalid_input () {
      echo "Invalid input '$REPLY'" >&2
      exit 1
}

read -p "Enter a single item > "

# input is empty (invalid)
[[ -z "$REPLY" ]] && invalid_input

# input is multiple items (invalid)
(( "$(echo "$REPLY" | wc -w)" > 1 )) && invalid_input

# is input a valid filename?
if [[ "$REPLY" =~ ^[-[:alnum:]\._]+$ ]]; then
      echo "'$REPLY' is a valid filename."
      ...
```

Inside the filename branch the script nests further tests: `[[ -e "$REPLY" ]]` for existence, and the patterns `^-?[[:digit:]]*\.[[:digit:]]+$` and `^-?[[:digit:]]+$` to tell a floating point number from an integer.

```

## Menus

In a menu-driven program the script divides into two parts: display the menu and read the answer, then carry out the chosen action:

```bash
#!/bin/bash

# read-menu: a menu driven system information program

clear
echo "
Please Select:

1. Display System Information
2. Display Disk Space
3. Display Home Space Utilization
0. Quit
"
read -p "Enter selection [0-3] > "

if [[ "$REPLY" =~ ^[0-3]$ ]]; then
      if [[ "$REPLY" == 0 ]]; then
            echo "Program terminated."
            exit
      fi
      if [[ "$REPLY" == 1 ]]; then
            echo "Hostname: $HOSTNAME"
            uptime
            exit
      fi
      if [[ "$REPLY" == 2 ]]; then
            df -h
            exit
      fi
      if [[ "$REPLY" == 3 ]]; then
            if [[ "$(id -u)" -eq 0 ]]; then
                   echo "Home Space Utilization (All Users)"
                   du -sh /home/*
            else
                   echo "Home Space Utilization ($USER)"
                   du -sh "$HOME"
            fi
            exit
      fi
else
      echo "Invalid entry." >&2
      exit 1
fi
```

The `exit` calls stop the script from running later code after an action.

## Let's Try: Number Guessing

The chapter's Extra Credit asks you to rewrite these programs with `test` instead of `[[ ]]`, using grep for the regular expressions. Combining `read`, `[ ]` and arithmetic also gives a number-guessing game:

```bash
#!/bin/sh
# guess-number: built from this chapter's tools

answer=42
read -p "Enter your guess > " guess

if [ "$guess" = "$answer" ]; then
      echo "Correct! You win."
elif [ "$guess" -lt "$answer" ]; then
      echo "Too low."
else
      echo "Too high."
fi
```

## Summary

- `read` stores one line of standard input into variables, or into `REPLY` when given no names.
- `-p`, `-n`, `-s` and `-t` add prompts, character counts, silent input, and timeouts.
- `IFS` controls field splitting, prefix assignments apply only to the following command, and `<<<` feeds a here string.
- Piping into read fails because subshells cannot alter the parent environment.
- Validate every input against empty values, extra words, and invalid characters.

# Chapter 29: Flow Control: Looping with while/until

Loops let a program repeat a series of steps until some condition is reached. This chapter introduces the shell's `while` and `until` compound commands, the `break` and `continue` commands that control flow inside a loop, and how to process a file line by line inside a loop.

## Looping

Life is full of repeated activities. Slicing a carrot, in pseudocode, lifts the knife, advances the carrot, and slices it, quitting when the carrot is finished; those steps form a **loop** that runs until a condition is met.

## while

`bash` expresses this idea with the `while` compound command:

```bash
while commands; do commands; done
```

Like `if`, `while` evaluates the exit status of a list of commands. As long as the exit status is zero it performs the commands inside the loop.

```bash
#!/bin/bash

# while-count: display a series of numbers

count=1

while [[ "$count" -le 5 ]]; do
      echo "$count"
      count=$((count + 1))
done
echo "Finished."
```

Run, it prints `1 2 3 4 5` then `Finished.` We can wrap the menu program from the previous chapter in a `while` loop so it repeats until the user chooses to quit:

```bash
#!/bin/bash

# while-menu: a menu driven system information program

DELAY=3 # Number of seconds to display results

while [[ "$REPLY" != 0 ]]; do
      clear
      cat <<- _EOF_
            Please Select:

              1. Display System Information
              2. Display Disk Space
              3. Display Home Space Utilization
              0. Quit

      _EOF_
      read -p "Enter selection [0-3] > "

      if [[ "$REPLY" =~ ^[0-3]$ ]]; then
            if [[ $REPLY == 1 ]]; then
                  echo "Hostname: $HOSTNAME"
                  uptime
                  sleep "$DELAY"
            fi
            if [[ "$REPLY" == 2 ]]; then
                  df -h
                  sleep "$DELAY"
            fi
            if [[ "$REPLY" == 3 ]]; then
                  if [[ "$(id -u)" -eq 0 ]]; then
                         echo "Home Space Utilization (All Users)"
                         du -sh /home/*
                  else
                         echo "Home Space Utilization ($USER)"
                         du -sh "$HOME"
                  fi
                  sleep "$DELAY"
            fi
      else
              echo "Invalid entry."
              sleep "$DELAY"
      fi
done
echo "Program terminated."
```

## Breaking Out of a Loop

`bash` provides two builtin commands to control flow inside loops. **break** immediately terminates a loop and resumes with the next statement after the loop. **continue** skips the rest of the current iteration and resumes with the next iteration. A common technique is an endless loop driven by `true`, which never ends on its own, so the programmer supplies a `break`:

```bash
while true; do
      read -p "Enter selection [0-3] > "
      if [[ "$REPLY" == 1 ]]; then
            echo "Hostname: $HOSTNAME"; uptime; sleep "$DELAY"; continue
      fi
      if [[ "$REPLY" == 0 ]]; then
            break
      fi
done
```

The `continue` at the end of each choice skips testing the remaining choices once one matches.

## until

The **until** command is like `while`, but it continues until it receives a zero exit status instead of until it receives a non-zero one:

```bash
#!/bin/bash

# until-count: display a series of numbers

count=1

until [[ "$count" -gt 5 ]]; do
      echo "$count"
      count=$((count + 1))
done
echo "Finished."
```

Choosing `while` or `until` is usually a matter of writing the clearest test.

## Reading Files with Loops

`while` and `until` can process standard input, so files can be read line by line. Place the redirection operator after `done`:

```bash
#!/bin/bash

# while-read: read lines from a file

while read distro version release; do
      printf "Distro: %s\tVersion: %s\tReleased: %s\n" "$distro" "$version" "$release"
done < distros.txt
```

`read` exits with a zero status after each line until end-of-file, when it exits non-zero and the loop ends. You can also pipe input into a loop:

```bash
#!/bin/bash

# while-read2: read lines from a file

sort -k 1,1 -k 2n distros.txt | while read distro version release; do
      printf "Distro: %s\tVersion: %s\tReleased: %s\n" "$distro" "$version" "$release"
done
```

Because a pipe runs the loop in a subshell, variables created inside the loop are lost when it terminates.

Note: on a POSIX shell such as `ash` (the guest VM default), `[[ ]]` and `=~` are bash-only. Use `[ "$count" -le 5 ]` for the same tests, or run scripts with `bash script.sh`.

## Summary

- `while` repeats its body as long as the test returns a zero exit status; `until` repeats until it does.
- `break` ends a loop; `continue` jumps to the next iteration.
- An endless `while true` loop is a common pattern; the programmer must add a `break`.
- `while read ... done < file` processes a file line by line.
- A piped loop runs in a subshell, so its variable assignments do not survive.

# Chapter 30: Troubleshooting

As scripts grow, things go wrong. This chapter looks at the two broad classes of errors, syntactic and logical, shows defensive programming habits, and demonstrates testing and debugging techniques such as tracing with `set -x`.

## Syntactic Errors

Syntactic errors involve mistyping shell syntax; the shell stops executing the script. We use this demonstration script:

```bash
#!/bin/bash

# trouble: script to demonstrate common errors

number=1

if [ $number = 1 ]; then
      echo "Number is equal to 1."
else
      echo "Number is not equal to 1."
fi
```

### Missing Quotes

Removing the closing quote from the first `echo` gives:

```
/home/me/bin/trouble: line 10: unexpected EOF while looking for matching `"'
/home/me/bin/trouble: line 13: syntax error: unexpected end of file
```

The reported line numbers are later than the real mistake because `bash` keeps hunting for the closing quote until it finds one after the second `echo`.

### Missing or Unexpected Tokens

Removing the `;` after the test in the `if` line gives:

```
/home/me/bin/trouble: line 9: syntax error near unexpected token `else'
```

Without the semicolon, `then` becomes another argument to `[`, and `else` is then read out of place as a reserved word.

### Unanticipated Expansions

Setting `number=` (empty) causes an intermittent failure:

```
/home/me/bin/trouble: line 7: [: =: unary operator expected
```

`[ $number = 1 ]` expands to `[   = 1 ]`, which is invalid. Quoting the variable fixes it:

```bash
[ "$number" = 1 ]
```

> Make it a rule to always enclose variables and command substitutions in double quotes unless word splitting is needed.

## Logical Errors

Logical errors do not stop the script but make it do the wrong thing. Common kinds are incorrect conditional expressions, "off by one" counting errors in loops, and unanticipated situations such as filenames with embedded spaces.

## Defensive Programming

Verify assumptions by checking exit statuses. A famous disaster script:

```bash
cd $dir_name
rm *
```

If `dir_name` is unset, `cd` fails and `rm` deletes the current directory. Improve it step by step:

```bash
cd "$dir_name" && rm *
```

Better still, test that the target is a real directory and report errors to standard error:

```bash
if [[ ! -d "$dir_name" ]]; then
      echo "No such directory: '$dir_name'" >&2
      exit 1
fi
if ! cd "$dir_name"; then
      echo "Cannot cd to '$dir_name'" >&2
      exit 1
fi
if ! rm ./*; then
      echo "File deletion failed. Check results" >&2
      exit 1
fi
```

Precede wildcards with `./` so a filename beginning with a hyphen is not read as an option. A POSIX portable filename uses only `A-Z a-z 0-9 . - _`.

## Verifying Input and Testing

If a program accepts input it must handle anything it receives; the menu test `[[ $REPLY =~ ^[0-3]$ ]]` is a good example. For testing, replace dangerous commands with `echo` (a stub) and mark the changes so they can be found and removed:

```bash
echo rm * # TESTING
```

Choose test cases that cover edge conditions: an existing directory, a nonexistent directory, and an empty variable.

## Debugging

Isolate the problem area by commenting out sections. Use tracing to see the actual flow of execution. Enable tracing for the whole script with `#!/bin/bash -x`, or for part of it with the `set` command:

```bash
#!/bin/bash
number=1
set -x # Turn on tracing
if [ $number = 1 ]; then
      echo "Number is equal to 1."
else
      echo "Number is not equal to 1."
fi
set +x # Turn off tracing
```

Trace output is prefixed with `+` (the `PS4` variable); `export PS4='$LINENO + '` adds the line number. Displaying variable values with `echo "number=$number" # DEBUG` is useful for watching loops and arithmetic.

## Summary

- Syntactic errors stop the script; error messages often point past the real mistake.
- Always quote variables and command substitutions unless you want word splitting.
- Logical errors give wrong results; guard against off-by-one and unanticipated data.
- Program defensively: check exit statuses, verify input, and send errors to standard error.
- Trace with `set -x`/`set +x` or `#!/bin/bash -x`; `PS4` controls the trace prefix.
- Test with stubs (`echo` before dangerous commands) and good test cases.

# Chapter 31: Flow Control: Branching with case

A series of `if` tests for mutually exclusive choices is clumsy. `bash` provides the `case` compound command for multiple-choice decisions, matching a word against patterns built from the same wildcards used by pathname expansion.

## The case Command

The syntax is:

```bash
case word in
      [pattern [| pattern]...) commands ;;]...
esac
```

The `case` command looks at `word` and tries to match it against each pattern. On the first match, the associated commands run and no further patterns are tested. Replacing the `if` chain in the menu program:

```bash
#!/bin/bash

# case-menu: a menu driven system information program

clear
echo "
Please Select:

1. Display System Information
2. Display Disk Space
3. Display Home Space Utilization
0. Quit
"
read -p "Enter selection [0-3] > "

case "$REPLY" in
     0)     echo "Program terminated."
            exit
            ;;
     1)     echo "Hostname: $HOSTNAME"
            uptime
            ;;
     2)     df -h
            ;;
     3)     if [[ "$(id -u)" -eq 0 ]]; then
                 echo "Home Space Utilization (All Users)"
                 du -sh /home/*
            else
                 echo "Home Space Utilization ($USER)"
                 du -sh "$HOME"
            fi
            ;;
     *)     echo "Invalid entry" >&2
            exit 1
            ;;
esac
```

## Patterns

Patterns are terminated with `)` and use pathname-expansion wildcards:

```
a)              word equals a.
[[:alpha:]])    word is a single alphabetic character.
???             word is exactly three characters long.
*.txt)          word ends with .txt.
*)              matches any value (good practice as the last pattern).
```

An example using classes and ranges:

```bash
#!/bin/bash
read -p "enter word > "
case "$REPLY" in
     [[:alpha:]])   echo "is a single alphabetic character." ;;
     [ABC][0-9])    echo "is A, B, or C followed by a digit." ;;
     ???)           echo "is three characters long." ;;
     *.txt)         echo "is a word ending in '.txt'" ;;
     *)             echo "is something else." ;;
esac
```

The vertical bar combines patterns into an "or", handy for matching both cases of a letter. Changing the menu to letters:

```bash
case "$REPLY" in
    q|Q)   echo "Program terminated."; exit ;;
    a|A)   echo "Hostname: $HOSTNAME"; uptime ;;
    b|B)   df -h ;;
    c|C)   # ... home usage ...
    *)     echo "Invalid entry" >&2; exit 1 ;;
esac
```

## Performing Multiple Actions

In `bash` before 4.0, a `case` terminated after one match. A `case4-1` character test therefore only reported the first matching class. Modern bash adds the `;;&` notation, which continues testing later patterns instead of stopping:

```bash
case "$REPLY" in
     [[:upper:]])   echo "'$REPLY' is upper case." ;;&
     [[:lower:]])   echo "'$REPLY' is lower case." ;;&
     [[:alpha:]])   echo "'$REPLY' is alphabetic." ;;&
     [[:digit:]])   echo "'$REPLY' is a digit." ;;&
esac
```

Running `case4-2` with `a` prints that it is lower case, alphabetic, a visible character, and a hexadecimal digit.

Note: `case`, `[[:class:]]` patterns and `*)` are POSIX and run fine under the guest's `ash`; only `;;&` is bash 4+.

## Summary

- `case word in pattern) commands ;; ... esac` handles multiple-choice decisions.
- Patterns use pathname wildcards and are ended by `)`.
- `*)` matches anything and is a good final catch-all.
- `|` combines patterns into an "or", e.g. `q|Q`.
- `;;&` (bash 4+) keeps testing further patterns after a match.

# Chapter 32: Positional Parameters

Scripts so far could not read their own command line. The shell exposes the words on the command line through **positional parameters**, letting programs accept arguments and options.

## Accessing the Command Line

The positional parameters are named `$0` through `$9`. `$0` always holds the pathname of the program itself; `$1`-`$9` hold the first through ninth arguments:

```bash
#!/bin/bash

# posit-param: script to view command line parameters

echo "
\$0 = $0
\$1 = $1
\$2 = $2
\$3 = $3
"
```

Run with arguments, `$1`, `$2`, `$3` are filled; empty ones show nothing. You can reach more than nine parameters with braces, e.g. `${10}`, `${55}`.

## Determining the Number of Arguments

The special variable `$#` holds the number of arguments on the command line.

## shift - Getting Access to Many Arguments

`shift` moves every parameter down one: `$2` becomes `$1`, `$3` becomes `$2`, and so on, and `$#` is reduced by one. `$0` never changes. Combined with a loop this processes any number of arguments:

```bash
#!/bin/bash

# posit-param2: script to display all arguments

count=1

while [[ $# -gt 0 ]]; do
      echo "Argument $count = $1"
      count=$((count + 1))
      shift
done
```

Even without `shift`, useful tools are possible. A simple file-information program uses `$1` and derives its own name from `$0`:

```bash
#!/bin/bash

# file-info: simple file information program

PROGNAME="$(basename "$0")"

if [[ -e "$1" ]]; then
      echo -e "\nFile Type:"
      file "$1"
      echo -e "\nFile Status:"
      stat "$1"
else
      echo "$PROGNAME: usage: $PROGNAME file" >&2
      exit 1
fi
```

`basename` strips the leading path from `$0`, so the usage message adapts if the script is renamed. Positional parameters also pass arguments into shell functions, where the `FUNCNAME` variable tracks the function's name.

## Handling Positional Parameters en Masse

Two special parameters expand to the whole list:

```
$*   All parameters. Quoted as "$*" it becomes ONE string,
     words joined by the first character of IFS.
$@   All parameters. Quoted as "$@" each parameter stays a
     separate word, as if individually double-quoted.
```

A demonstration:

```bash
#!/bin/bash
print_params () { echo "\$1 = $1"; echo "\$2 = $2"; }
pass_params () {
      echo '$* :';   print_params $*
      echo '"$*" :'; print_params "$*"
      echo '$@ :';   print_params $@
      echo '"$@" :'; print_params "$@"
}
pass_params "word" "words with spaces"
```

Only `"$@"` preserves the integrity of each parameter (here a two-word result), so it is the most useful form and should be used unless there is a reason not to.

## A More Complete Application

The classic pattern for command line options is a `while` loop over the parameters with a `case` inside, and a `shift` at the bottom:

```bash
# process command line options
while [[ -n "$1" ]]; do
      case "$1" in
            -f | --file)        shift; filename="$1" ;;
            -i | --interactive) interactive=1 ;;
            -h | --help)        usage; exit ;;
            *)                  usage >&2; exit 1 ;;
      esac
      shift
done
```

The loop runs while `$1` is not empty. When `-f` is seen, an extra `shift` advances `$1` to the filename it takes. The rest of `sys_info_page` turns report code into shell functions and redirects `write_html_page` to a chosen file after testing it is writable with `touch`.

Note: under `ash`, `$1`-`$9`, `$#`, `shift`, `$*` and `$@` all work. Replace `[[ ... ]]` with `[ ... ]` for POSIX, e.g. `while [ $# -gt 0 ]`.

## Summary

- Positional parameters `$1`-`$9` (and `${10}` ...) hold the command line words; `$0` is the program.
- `$#` is the argument count.
- `shift` moves parameters down so a loop can process any number.
- `basename "$0"` gives a rename-proof program name.
- `"$@"` keeps each parameter separate and is the safest way to pass them on.
- Option parsing is a `while` loop with `case` and `shift`.

# Chapter 33: Flow Control: Looping with for

The `for` loop differs from `while`/`until` by processing **sequences**. `bash` offers two forms: the traditional shell form and a C-language form.

## for: Traditional Shell Form

```bash
for variable [in words]; do
      commands
done
```

`variable` takes each item of `words` in turn; `commands` run on every iteration. It is handy on the command line:

```bash
for i in A B C D; do echo $i; done
```

The real power is in how the list of words is created. **Brace expansion** generates a range:

```bash
for i in {A..D}; do echo $i; done
```

**Pathname expansion** gives a clean file list, but check that the glob matched:

```bash
for i in distros*.txt; do
      if [[ -e "$i" ]]; then
            echo "$i"
      fi
done
```

**Command substitution** can also build the list. This program finds the longest word in a file using `strings` (a GNU binutils tool):

```bash
#!/bin/bash

# longest-word: find longest string in a file

while [[ -n "$1" ]]; do
      if [[ -r "$1" ]]; then
            max_word=
            max_len=0
            for i in $(strings "$1"); do
                  len="$(echo -n "$i" | wc -c)"
                  if (( len > max_len )); then
                        max_len="$len"
                        max_word="$i"
                  fi
            done
            echo "$1: '$max_word' ($max_len characters)"
      fi
      shift
done
```

Here `$(strings "$1")` is deliberately unquoted so word splitting produces the list. If `in words` is omitted, `for` iterates over the positional parameters:

```bash
#!/bin/bash
# longest-word2: find longest string in a file
for i; do
      if [[ -r "$i" ]]; then
            max_word=
            max_len=0
            for j in $(strings "$i"); do
                  len="$(echo -n "$j" | wc -c)"
                  if (( len > max_len )); then
                        max_len="$len"
                        max_word="$j"
                  fi
            done
            echo "$i: '$max_word' ($max_len characters)"
      fi
done
```

The loop variable is traditionally `i` (then `j`, `k`), a habit inherited from Fortran.

## for: C Language Form

Recent bash adds a second form resembling C:

```bash
for (( expression1; expression2; expression3 )); do
      commands
done
```

It is equivalent to running `expression1` to initialize, testing `expression2` before each pass, and running `expression3` at the end of each pass:

```bash
#!/bin/bash

# simple_counter: demo of C style for command

for (( i=0; i<5; i=i+1 )); do
      echo $i
done
```

This prints `0 1 2 3 4`, useful whenever a numeric sequence is needed.

The chapter closes by upgrading `report_home_space` to use a `for` loop over `$dir_list`, computing per-directory file and directory counts with `find | wc -l` and `du -sh | cut -f 1`, and formatting with `printf`.

Note: brace expansion `{A..D}`, the `(( ))` arithmetic test, and the C-style `for (( ))` are **bash-only**. Under the guest's `ash`, use an explicit list (`for i in 1 2 3 4 5`) or a `while [ "$i" -lt 5 ]` counter instead.

## Summary

- `for variable in words; do ...; done` iterates over a list of words.
- The list can come from brace expansion, pathname globbing, or command substitution.
- Guard a glob by testing that the file exists (`[[ -e "$i" ]]`).
- Omitting `in words` makes `for` loop over the positional parameters (`for i; do`).
- The C-style `for (( init; test; step ))` is bash-only and best for numeric sequences.

lessons.description: Manipulate strings with parameter expansions, do integer arithmetic with $(( )), and reach for bc when you need floating-point numbers.
lessons.content:
# Chapter 34: Strings and Numbers

Programs work with data at smaller units than files. This chapter covers shell **parameter expansions** for strings and **arithmetic expansion** for numbers, plus the external `bc` calculator for floating-point math.

## Parameter Expansion

The simplest expansion is a variable, optionally braced when adjacent text would confuse the shell: `${a}_file`. Positional parameters above nine use braces: `${11}`.

### Managing Empty Variables

```bash
${parameter:-word}   # word if parameter unset or empty
${parameter:=word}   # also assigns word to parameter (not for special params)
${parameter:?word}   # exit with error word if empty
${parameter:+word}   # word only if parameter is set and non-empty
```

```bash
foo=
echo ${foo:-"substitute value if unset"}   # prints the substitute
```

`${!prefix*}` returns the names of variables starting with `prefix`, e.g. `${!BASH*}`.

### String Operations

```bash
${#parameter}                 # length of the string
${parameter:offset:length}    # substring (bash-only; negative offset needs a space)
${parameter#pattern}          # remove shortest leading match   (## longest)
${parameter%pattern}          # remove shortest trailing match  (%% longest)
${parameter/pattern/string}   # replace first match (// all, /# start, /% end)
```

```bash
foo=file.txt.zip
echo ${foo#*.}     # txt.zip   (shortest)
echo ${foo##*.}    # zip       (longest)
echo ${foo%.*}     # file.txt
echo ${foo%%.*}    # file
foo=JPG.JPG
echo ${foo//JPG/jpg}   # jpg.jpg
```

These expansions replace external commands like `sed` and `cut` and are far faster. Rewriting `longest-word` to use `${#j}` instead of `$(echo -n $j | wc -c)` cut a run from 3.618s to 0.060s under `time`.

### Case Conversion

`declare -u upper` and `declare -l lower` force a variable to upper/lowercase. Four expansions do the same per use (bash-only):

```bash
${parameter,,}   all lowercase
${parameter,}    first char lowercase
${parameter^^}   all uppercase
${parameter^}    first char uppercase (capitalize)
```

## Arithmetic Evaluation and Expansion

Arithmetic expansion uses `$((expression))`; the `(( ))` compound command does truth tests. Integers may be written in other bases: `0number` octal, `0xnumber` hex, `base#number`.

```
Operators:  +  -  *  / (integer division)  ** (power)  % (remainder)
Assignment: = += -= *= /= %=  and ++ / -- (pre/post increment)
Bitwise:    ~ << >> & | ^
Logic:      <= >= < > == != && ||  and expr1?expr2:expr3 (ternary)
```

```bash
echo $(( 5 / 2 ))   # 2
echo $(( 5 % 2 ))   # 1
echo $((0xff))      # 255
for ((i = 0; i <= 20; ++i)); do
      if (( (i % 5) == 0 )); then printf "<%d> " "$i"; else printf "%d " "$i"; fi
done
```

In `(( ))` a value of zero is false and non-zero is true; `=` assigns while `==` compares.

## bc - An Arbitrary Precision Calculator

The shell does only integer math; for floating point use `bc`. A bc script uses C-style `/* */` comments and runs with `bc -q file.bc`, `bc < file.bc`, or via a **here string** `bc <<< "2+2"`. The `scale` variable sets precision. A loan-payment script:

```bash
#!/bin/bash

# loan-calc: script to calculate monthly loan payments

PROGNAME="${0##*/}"
usage () { cat <<- EOF
Usage: $PROGNAME PRINCIPAL INTEREST MONTHS
EOF
}

if (($# != 3)); then usage; exit 1; fi
principal=$1
interest=$2
months=$3

bc <<- EOF
      scale = 10
      i = $interest / 12
      p = $principal
      n = $months
      a = p * ((i * ((1 + i) ^ n)) / (((1 + i) ^ n) - 1))
      print a, "\n"
EOF
```

Note: `bc` may be absent on the guest. `$(( ))` integer math and `${#var}` lengths are POSIX and work under `ash`; substring `${var:off:len}`, case-conversion, `(( ))`, `<<<` and base prefixes are bash-only (run with `bash`).

## Summary

- `${parameter:-word}`, `:?`, `:=`, `:+` handle empty and missing variables.
- `${#var}`, `${var/pat/str}`, `${var#pat}` and `${var%pat}` manipulate strings faster than external tools.
- Case conversion: `declare -u/-l` and `${var^^}`, `${var,,}` (bash-only).
- `$(( ))` does integer arithmetic, including bases, `++/--`, bitwise and ternary operators.
- For floating point, pipe a script to `bc` and set `scale`; here strings pass it easily.

lessons.content:
# Chapter 35: Arrays

Scalar variables hold one value; an **array** holds many. `bash` supports one-dimensional arrays (and, from version 4, associative arrays). Array support first appeared in bash 2; the original `sh` had none.

## Creating an Array

Elements are addressed by an index called a **subscript**, starting at zero. An array is created simply by assigning to an element:

```bash
a[1]=foo
echo ${a[1]}      # braces are required to avoid pathname expansion
```

Or declare it explicitly: `declare -a a`.

## Assigning Values

Single element: `name[subscript]=value`. Several at once:

```bash
days=(Sun Mon Tue Wed Thu Fri Sat)
days=([0]=Sun [1]=Mon [2]=Tue [3]=Wed [4]=Thu [5]=Fri [6]=Sat)
```

## Accessing Elements

The `hours` script counts files by the hour they were last modified, using an array indexed 0-23:

```bash
#!/bin/bash

# hours: script to count files by modification time

usage () { echo "usage: ${0##*/} directory" >&2; }

if [[ ! -d "$1" ]]; then usage; exit 1; fi

# Initialize array
for i in {0..23}; do hours[i]=0; done

# Collect data
for i in $(stat -c %y "$1"/* | cut -c 12-13); do
      j="${i#0}"
      ((++hours[j]))
      ((++count))
done

# Display data
echo -e "Hour\tFiles\tHour\tFiles"
echo -e "----\t-----\t----\t-----"
for i in {0..11}; do
      j=$((i + 12))
      printf "%02d\t%d\t%02d\t%d\n" "$i" "${hours[i]}" "$j" "${hours[j]}"
done
printf "\nTotal files = %d\n" $count
```

## Array Operations

```bash
${a[*]}     all elements, one word when quoted
${a[@]}     all elements, separate words when quoted  (usually best)
${#a[@]}    number of elements in the array
${#a[100]}  length of one element
${!a[@]}    the list of subscripts actually in use
a+=(x y)    append values to the end of the array
unset a     delete the whole array; unset 'a[2]' deletes one element
```

An element exists only if it was assigned, so `a[100]=foo` reports `${#a[@]}` as 1. Note that `foo=` (empty assignment) does NOT clear an array - only element zero is emptied. To sort an array, feed it through a pipeline:

```bash
a=(f e d c b a)
a_sorted=($(for i in "${a[@]}"; do echo $i; done | sort))
echo "${a_sorted[@]}"
```

## Associative Arrays

`bash` 4.0+ supports arrays indexed by strings. They must be created with `declare -A`:

```bash
declare -A colors
colors["red"]="#ff0000"
colors["green"]="#00ff00"
echo ${colors["blue"]}
```

Arrays and loops pair naturally, especially with `for (( expr; expr; expr ))`.

Note: indexed arrays, `declare -a/-A`, `${a[@]}`, `${!a[@]}`, `+=` append and `(( ))` are all **bash-only**. The guest's `ash` has no arrays - use `set -- v1 v2 v3` to hold a list and iterate `for x in "$@"`, or run the array scripts with `bash /root/script.sh` if bash is installed.

## Summary

- An array holds multiple values addressed by a zero-based subscript.
- Create one by assignment or with `declare -a`; assign many at once with `name=(v1 v2 ...)`.
- `${a[@]}` (quoted) yields each element as a separate word; `${#a[@]}` counts elements.
- `${!a[@]}` lists used subscripts; `a+=(...)` appends; `unset a` deletes.
- Associative arrays (`declare -A`) use string indexes and need bash 4+.
- Everything here is bash-only; POSIX `sh`/`ash` lacks arrays.

lessons.content:
# Chapter 36: Exotica

The final chapter tours a handful of `bash` features that are less common but handy for particular problems: grouping commands and subshells, process substitution, signal traps, asynchronous execution, and named pipes.

## Group Commands and Subshells

`bash` runs a set of commands together in one of two ways:

```bash
{ command1; command2; }     # group command
( command1; command2 )      # subshell
```

The difference matters: a group command runs in the **current** shell, so variable assignments survive; a subshell runs in a child copy whose environment is thrown away. Group commands are therefore faster and use less memory, and are preferred unless isolation is wanted. Both manage redirection as a unit:

```bash
{ ls -l; echo "Listing of foo.txt"; cat foo.txt; } > output.txt
(ls -l; echo "Listing of foo.txt"; cat foo.txt) > output.txt
{ ls -l; echo "Listing of foo.txt"; cat foo.txt; } | lpr
```

Note the braces need spaces around them and a terminating `;` before `}`. The `array-2` script ties this together with an associative array to tally file owners, wrapping each reporting loop in `{ ... } | sort`.

## Process Substitution

Because pipeline stages run in subshells, `echo "foo" | read` leaves `$REPLY` empty - the `read` happened in a subshell that then died. **Process substitution** works around this by treating a command's output as a file:

```bash
<(list)   # output of list as a file
>(list)   # input to list as a file
```

```bash
read < <(echo "foo")
echo $REPLY
```

The expansion is a real filename; `echo <(echo "foo")` prints something like `/dev/fd/63`. A classic use is a `read` loop over a command's output without losing variables:

```bash
#!/bin/bash

# pro-sub: demo of process substitution

while read attr links owner group size date time filename; do
      cat << EOF
Filename:   $filename
Size:       $size
Owner:      $owner
Group:      $group
Modified:   $date $time
Links:      $links
EOF
done < <(ls -l | tail -n +2)
```

## Traps

Scripts can respond to signals with the `trap` builtin:

```bash
trap argument signal [signal...]
```

A simple example prints a message instead of stopping on ctrl-C:

```bash
#!/bin/bash
# trap-demo: simple signal handling demo
trap "echo 'I am ignoring you.'" SIGINT SIGTERM
for i in {1..5}; do
      echo "Iteration $i of 5"
      sleep 5
done
```

It is cleaner to trap to a shell function, and each handler should usually `exit`:

```bash
#!/bin/bash
exit_on_signal_SIGINT () { echo "Script interrupted." 2>&1; exit 0; }
exit_on_signal_SIGTERM () { echo "Script terminated." 2>&1; exit 0; }
trap exit_on_signal_SIGINT SIGINT
trap exit_on_signal_SIGTERM SIGTERM
```

Signal handlers are often used to delete temporary files. Create unpredictable names with `mktemp /tmp/foobar.$$.XXXXXXXXXX` rather than `$RANDOM` alone.

## Asynchronous Execution with wait

A script can run child scripts in the background with `&`. The `wait` command pauses the parent until a given PID finishes. `$!` holds the PID of the last background job:

```bash
async-child &
pid=$!
# ... parent keeps working ...
wait "$pid"
```

## Named Pipes

A **named pipe** (FIFO) connects two processes through a filesystem entry, created with `mkfifo`:

```bash
mkfifo pipe1
ls -l > pipe1      # blocks until a reader attaches
cat < pipe1        # receives the ls output
```

`process1 > named_pipe` plus `process2 < named_pipe` behaves like `process1 | process2`.

Note: group commands `{ ...; }`, subshells `( ... )`, ordinary heredocs (`<< EOF`), `trap`, `wait`, `$!` and `mkfifo` all work under the guest's `ash`. Process substitution `<(...)`, here strings `<<<`, and brace ranges `{1..5}` are **bash-only**.

## Summary

- `{ cmds; }` groups in the current shell; `( cmds )` groups in a subshell that discards variable changes - prefer group commands when it does not matter.
- Group commands and subshells let you redirect or pipe a whole set of commands at once.
- Process substitution `<(list)` avoids the lost-variable problem of `read` in a pipeline (bash-only).
- `trap command SIGNAL` lets a script handle signals, e.g. to clean up temporary files.
- Run jobs with `&`, record `$!`, and synchronize with `wait`.
- `mkfifo` creates a named pipe so two processes can talk like `process1 | process2`.
